Dieu explique que si un homme ou une femme meurt sans enfant ni père ni mère et laisse une sœur germaine ou consanguine, celle-ci reçoit la moitié de la succession, et le frère hérite d'elle s'il n'y a pas d'enfant pour elle. Si il y a deux sœurs, elles reçoivent les deux tiers, et lorsque frères et sœurs sont réunis, le garçon reçoit la part de deux filles. Les commentateurs rapportent que, selon Abu Bakr, la kalala désigne celui qui n'a ni enfant ni parent, tandis que d'autres, comme Umar dans certaines transmissions, la limitent à l'absence de père. Ibn Kathir indique que l'avis de la majorité est qu'il faut l'absence des deux, descendants et ascendants. Tous s'accordent à dire que la sœur n'hérite pas en présence du père. En revanche, Ibn Abbas et ceux qui le suivent, dont Dawud al-Zahiri, estiment que la sœur n'hérite pas aux côtés d'une fille, alors que la majorité, dont Ibn Mas'ud et Mu'adh, lui accorde la moitié par la voie de l'agnation. Al-Tabari rapporte qu'Umar regrettait la difficulté de cette question et souhaitait que le Prophète l'eût tranchée de son vivant. Sur la formule finale, les grammairiens divergent : les Basriyyun comprennent « de peur que vous ne vous égariez », tandis que les Kufiyyun y voient une négation sous-entendue, ce que retient la plupart des commentateurs.
en: The verse opens with a general address to all people, urging them to be mindful of their Lord, who created them from a single soul, Adam, made his spouse, Eve, from it, and spread from the two a great multitude of men and women. The commentators draw from this that all humankind shares one origin, so people must show mutual kindness and compassion and uphold each other's rights. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Abbas, report that Eve was made from one of Adam's ribs, relying on the authentic hadith that woman was created from a rib. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, and al-Zamakhshari in one of his two readings, understand 'from it' to mean 'from its kind'. The verse then repeats the command to fear God and to keep the ties of kinship. The readers differ on the case of 'the wombs': most read it in the accusative, linking it to God's name, while Hamza reads it in the genitive, linking it to the preceding pronoun. The Basran grammarians consider the genitive reading faulty, while the Kufans and Ibn Malik accept it. Many explain that to 'ask one another by' means to request something by God and by the ties of kinship. The verse ends by affirming that God is watchful over them, a warning against disobedience.

This verse commands guardians to hand over orphans' property when they reach maturity, not to swap the bad of the orphans' wealth for the good of their own, and not to mix the orphans' property with their own and consume it together, since this is a grave sin. The commentators largely agree that 'the bad' and 'the good' mean the unlawful and the lawful. Al-Tabari reports that Mujahid understood it as taking the unlawful in place of the lawful, and others as hastening to eat unlawful gain before the lawful provision that God has allotted arrives. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Zuhri, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak take it as giving a worn or false coin or a thin animal in place of the better one. Ibn Zayd reports that the pre-Islamic Arabs did not pass inheritance to women or young children, which was an injustice. Al-Tabari finds this view untenable because exchange requires one thing to replace another, and he prefers the concrete sense of swapping goods as most fitting the context of orphans. Ibn Kathir cites the same exchange of sheep and dirhams. The preposition 'ila' is read by several scholars as meaning 'with', while the more skilled grammarians keep its sense of addition. 'Hawb' means sin, and the pronoun 'innahu' refers to the act of consuming. On when the property is to be returned, most hold that it is after puberty and the proof of sound judgement, while some understand 'giving' as safeguarding the wealth so that no harm comes to it.

This verse addresses guardians of orphan girls: if they fear they will not be fair to them, they should marry other women of their choice. Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada, explain that just as one fears injustice towards orphans, one should also fear injustice towards wives. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate the report of 'A'isha: a man would marry the orphan in his care for her wealth and beauty without giving her a fair dowry, so this was forbidden. Mujahid reads the verse as a warning against fornication, following the caution against consuming orphans' property. The phrase 'what pleases you' generally means what is lawful; al-Tabari notes that 'ma' refers to the act of marriage rather than to the persons. 'Two, three or four' means, according to most, that each may marry two, three or four women, not nine in total; Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari hold that the limit of four applies to free men, the exception being specific to the Prophet. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa restrict a slave to two wives, while Malik allows him four. 'One, or what your right hands possess' means being content with one wife or taking slave concubines, with no obligation of equal treatment towards them according to the majority. The meaning of 'not to deviate' (ta'ulu) is debated: most render it as 'not to be unjust or biased', while al-Shafi'i understands it as 'not to have too many dependants', an interpretation most linguists reject though some find it acceptable.

This verse commands men to give women their dowry as a binding obligation, a gift owed in full. The commentators differ on who is addressed. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Juraij and Ibn Zayd, followed by al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj, understand the husbands, while Abu Salih, al-Kalbi and Mujahid understand the guardians, who in pre-Islamic times took the bride-price for themselves. All agree that the dowry belongs to the woman and should be paid willingly. On the word nihla, Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it to mean an obligatory fixed portion, al-Kalbi a gift, al-Zajjaj a matter of religious duty, and Abu Ubayda a gift given with a willing heart.

The rest of the verse, that if the women willingly give up part of it, you may enjoy it with ease and without harm, is understood by most to mean that if she freely and without coercion or deception relinquishes some of her dowry, the husband may take it without guilt. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the pronoun to refer to the dowry, and Ibn Kathir and several early scholars add that there is no blame in this world or the next. Jurists differ on whether a woman may take back such a gift: most hold it is final, while Shurayh and Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan allowed her to retract, arguing that a truly willing soul would not take it back, a view also reported from Umar. The words hanian and marian describe something pleasant to swallow whose outcome is sound.

God commands guardians not to hand over the wealth He made a means of support to the foolish, who cannot manage it well, but to provide for them from it, clothe them, and speak to them kindly. The commentators differ on who the foolish are. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Malik, al-Zuhri and Ibn Zayd take them to be children or orphans, while Mujahid and Ibn 'Umar take them to be women. Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn 'Abbas include both women and children. Al-Tabari holds that the verse is general, covering anyone deserving restriction for poor handling of money, and argues that limiting it to women conflicts with Arabic usage. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also take it to cover anyone unable to protect property, whether child, woman or adult. Most explain the phrase about providing from the wealth as meaning that the guardian should invest it in trade so that the upkeep comes from profits rather than from the capital. For the phrase about kind speech, the views range from a pleasant promise and a blessing to gentle tone, and Ibn Juraij says it means promising to hand the property back once the person matures.

This verse tells guardians to test orphans before they reach marriageable age, to see whether they can manage and preserve their property. When they reach that age and their sound judgment is evident, their wealth is handed over. The commentators read the test as examining the orphan's reason and conduct, the marriageable age as puberty or the required age, and rushd as good sense and sound management of property, with some including religious uprightness. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi note that this sound judgment can only appear after puberty, and that if it is absent the guardianship continues. Abu Hanifa holds that a period after puberty is sufficient, while the majority require the judgment itself to be proven. The text forbids consuming orphans' property through extravagance or by hurrying before they grow up. A wealthy guardian should abstain, and a poor one may take what is reasonable. Here Umar, Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Sha'bi read it as a loan to be repaid when he is able, al-Hasan and others as a wage or bare necessity with no repayment, and al-Nakha'i and Ata' as requiring no repayment at all. The verse ends by ordering witnesses at the handover, with God as sufficient witness over all this.

This verse establishes that men and women alike have a legitimate share in what parents and relatives leave behind, whether the estate is small or large, and that this share is fixed and obligatory. The commentators report that pre-Islamic Arabs did not pass inheritance to women or children, and that the verse came to abolish this custom. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others relate the story of Umm Kuhha, her daughters and the deceased's paternal cousins, though the names and details differ between accounts. Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn Abbas and others regard the verse as still in force, while Qatada and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab hold it abrogated by the inheritance verses, and some say the ruling is a recommendation rather than an obligation.

The commentators agree that the exact shares are detailed in the inheritance verses that follow, and that this verse states the principle in general terms. Al-Razi argues that distant relatives are not included, since no fixed share exists for them, whereas the Hanafis and Imamis cite the verse to grant them inheritance rights. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi discuss the grammatical nuances of the phrase nasiban mafrudan.

The following verse instructs that those present at the division who are not heirs, such as relatives, orphans and the needy, should be given something from the estate and spoken to kindly. Scholars differ on whether this is obligatory or recommended, and on what should be done when some heirs are minors. The passage also strongly condemns wrongfully consuming the property of orphans.

This verse says that relatives who do not inherit, along with orphans and the poor, who attend the division of an estate should be given something from it and addressed with kind words. The commentators differ on its status. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrima, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan and al-Zuhri hold that it is a firm, unabrogated ruling. For Mujahid the gift is obligatory to the extent that the heirs are willing, while others take it as a recommendation. A report from Ibn 'Abbas says that if some heirs are minors, the guardian apologises, explaining that the property belongs to the children. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Malik, al-Dahhak and Qatada say it was abrogated by the inheritance verses. Al-Tabari reads the division as one of bequests and rejects abrogation. Al-Mawardi, al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi generally treat the giving as a recommended kindness that consoles the needy. 'Ubayda and Ibn Sirin are reported to have prepared a meal from a sheep taken from the estate. The kind word is explained as a prayer for these people, a courteous apology for a small share, or the phrase "may God bless you". The commentators stress gentleness of speech and the avoidance of reproach, humiliation or reminders of favour.

This verse calls people to fear God and to show care for weak descendants: those who attend a dying person or guard orphans should fear for others' children as they would fear for their own if they were left vulnerable. The commentators agree on the core meaning: protect the rights of the weak and speak to them with justice and gentleness. They differ, however, on who is addressed. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari, al-Suddi, Mujahid, Qatada, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak take it to mean those present at a testator's bedside, who should dissuade him from squandering his wealth in ways that harm his heirs and urge him to leave his property to his children. Miqsam and al-Hadrami reverse this: some present persuade the dying man not to bequeath anything to relatives, and the verse forbids this. Al-Kalbi, and a report from Ibn 'Abbas, apply it to guardians of orphans, who should treat them as they would want their own children treated after them. Ibn Kathir reports that al-Tabari preferred a reading about bequests rather than inheritance, holding that the verse concerns wills that do not harm weak heirs. On the preceding verse, Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes hold it to be muhkam, while Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Qatada consider it abrogated by the inheritance verses. Several scholars cite the Prophet's words to Sa'd: a third is much. The qawl sadid is a sound, fair word.

This verse states that those who unjustly consume the property of orphans are, in truth, only eating fire into their bellies, since what they consume leads them to the Fire, and they will burn in the blazing Fire. The commentators agree that the threat covers anyone who takes an orphan's property unjustly, and that mentioning the bellies adds emphasis and vividness, the verb 'eat' standing for the most common use of wealth. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi take the fire as a reality of the Hereafter, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan explain the word 'fire' as meaning what leads to the Fire, with Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir also presenting the literal sense. Several works, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, cite the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri about the night journey, in which men with camel-like lips have stones of fire forced into their mouths, but the commentators note that the transmitter Abu Harun al-Abdi is weak. Al-Suddi describes the one who consumes such wealth being raised on the Day of Resurrection with flames issuing from his mouth and eyes. The word 'unjustly' is understood by most as 'without right', which excludes the lawful consumption of a poor guardian's fair wage, as al-Razi and al-Qurtubi point out. The word sa'ir means a blazing fire, and the passive reading 'yuslawna', attributed to Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, is noted beside the majority reading. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi remark that this is a verse of warning, and that according to Sunni belief the punishment may not apply to every sinner. The reports on the occasion of revelation differ: some name a man from Ghatafan, others Hanzala ibn al-Shamardal, and Ibn Zayd considers it addressed to unbelievers who did not give inheritance to women and children.

The commentators explain that this verse prescribes, for children after their parents' death, that a son receive the share of two daughters. If there are more than two daughters, they receive two-thirds; if there is one, she receives half. Most scholars, including al-Tabari, hold that two daughters also take two-thirds, while Ibn 'Abbas gave them half, a view some report he later abandoned. Parents each take a sixth when there is a child; without a child, if only the parents inherit, the mother takes a third and the father the rest. When a spouse is present, opinions differ: al-Tabari and most companions and jurists give the spouse their share first and then the mother a third of the remainder, whereas Ibn 'Abbas gives her a third of the whole estate. If the deceased leaves two or more siblings, they reduce the mother's share to a sixth; most count two siblings, Ibn 'Abbas requires three, and there is debate over who takes that sixth, the father according to most, the siblings according to Ibn 'Abbas.

The commentators note that bequests and debts come before division, the bequest being limited to a third and not made to an heir; the debt, though mentioned after the bequest, takes precedence. They also note the wisdom of the text: no one knows which of their parents or children will be most beneficial to them, so God Himself fixed the shares. The division is a divine prescription, full of knowledge and wisdom, to which one must submit. The commentators add that the verse's general logic, along with the rules of kalala, clarifies the sense of inheritance as a whole.

This passage of Surat al-Nisa' sets the shares of the spouses: the husband receives half of what his wife leaves if she has no child, and a quarter if she has one; the wife receives a quarter of what her husband leaves if he has no child, and an eighth if he has one. Debts and bequests are settled before the inheritance is divided. Kalala denotes a person who leaves neither father nor child; his maternal brother or sister then receives a sixth each, and if there are several they share the third equally. The commentators explain that kalala means what lies beyond the parent and the child, the view of Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, and of the majority; a different opinion attributed to Ibn Abbas and Umar was later abandoned by them. Some take the word to mean the heirs, the inherited property or kinship in general. All agree that the siblings meant are those through the mother, as Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas's reading confirms. Several note that a bequest made to harm the heirs is invalid and cannot exceed a third. The scholars differ on questions such as 'awl, the grandfather alongside brothers, and the case known as al-himariyya: the majority have the maternal siblings share the third with full siblings, while Ali, Ibn Abbas and others disagree.

This verse calls the rules just stated about orphans, bequests and inheritance the "limits of God", that is, the laws that must not be overstepped. The commentators give the word several close meanings. Al-Suddi takes them to be conditions, Ibn 'Abbas to be obedience, and others understand them as statutes or obligations. Ibn Kathir notes that these explanations amount to the same thing. Al-Tabari, however, holds that a limit is what separates two things, so the prescribed division forms a boundary between obedience to God and disobedience to Him.

The second part states the reward of those who obey God and His Messenger: they will be admitted into gardens with rivers flowing beneath them, to remain there forever. This triumph is described as a great success, which al-Tabari explains as salvation and lasting enjoyment of bounty. The commentators agree that obedience here means respecting the rules of inheritance and the other commands, and that eternal life in Paradise is the recompense.

Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan add that obedience and disobedience cover both carrying out commands and refraining from prohibitions. They also observe that the verse begins with the reward of the obedient, which suits the good news it conveys. Ibn Juzayy, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi stress the figurative sense of limits, which one may not exceed.

The readings differ on the verb "He will admit him": Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it in the first person plural, the others in the third person. The word "abiding" is treated as a circumstantial state by al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, and its sense of eternity is upheld unless something indicates otherwise.

This verse states that whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, meaning the rules He set especially for inheritance, will be admitted by Allah into the Fire to remain in it forever, and will suffer a humiliating punishment. Al-Tabari explains that the disobedience here is the violation of what was commanded or forbidden in dividing estates. He adds that eternal abiding applies to one who, besides disobeying, doubts or rejects God's ruling and thus becomes a disbeliever outside Islam, whereas Ibn Abbas links the disobedience to the inheritance rules just mentioned. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report that the Mu'tazila used this verse to argue that sinning believers will remain in Hell forever; the Sunni scholars reply that it concerns the disbeliever who transgresses all the limits, and that the threat is conditional on the absence of repentance and divine forgiveness. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur note that khulud may mean a very long duration rather than eternity when the sin is not disbelief. The commentators agree that the verse belongs to the register of promise and warning that follows the statement of God's limits, which must not be crossed. Al-Alusi observes that the humiliating punishment combines bodily and spiritual suffering. Al-Baydawi and al-Jalalayn draw attention to the grammar of the passage, where agreement shifts between singular and plural.

This verse concerns a woman who commits adultery among the believing women. It requires four Muslim witnesses against her; if they testify, she is kept confined in the houses until death takes her or God makes a way for her. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur, agree that this ruling belonged to the early period of Islam and was abrogated or clarified by the prescribed penalty. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the way God made is the hundred lashes and exile for the unmarried, and the hundred lashes with stoning for the married, based on the hadith of 'Ubada ibn al-Samit. For the next verse, most exegetes take it to refer to the two offenders, with the harm meaning rebuke, censure and striking with sandals, later replaced by the legal penalty. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur hold that the first verse concerns confinement, while az-Zamakhshari and others take the way to be marriage; the majority take it to be the legal penalty. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, as reported by al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, held that the first verse concerns women who engage in lesbianism and the second men, a view most scholars rejected. Some commentators treat the confinement as an abrogated punishment, and scholars debated whether it was a penalty or a threat of one. All agree that repentance and reform lead to leaving the offenders alone, and that God is the Oft-Returning, the Most Merciful.

This verse concerns indecency, that is fornication, and sets out the punishment of the offenders at the beginning of the legislation. The commentators' plain reading is that women who commit this indecency, when four Muslims testify against them, are confined to their houses until death or until God makes a way for them, while the two who commit it are to be blamed and reproached; if they repent and amend their conduct, they are to be left alone, for God is Oft-Returning and Merciful. The exegetes agree that this ruling was later abrogated: Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report the scholars' consensus that it was abrogated by the flogging verse in Surat al-Nur and by the Sunna for stoning and exile. They differ on the nature of the reproach: Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others take it to mean insults, rebuke and beating with sandals, while Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi limit it to verbal reproach. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, followed by Mujahid in one transmission, applies the first verse to female homosexuality and the second to male homosexuality, whereas the majority take both as fornicators. They also differ on the meaning of 'the two': al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd understand virgins, 'Ata' and al-Hasan a man and a woman, and al-Tabari prefers that the verse concerns virgin men and women. Some regard confinement as a temporary penalty, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi allow that it may not be abrogated and may be a protective measure. Repentance remains the condition for lifting the reproach.

This verse states that accepting repentance is a matter of God's grace, which He has made binding upon Himself, and that He accepts it from those who do wrong out of ignorance, meaning heedlessness and the pull of desire rather than defiance, and who repent soon after. The commentators agree that sin is called ignorance because the sinner did not weigh its consequences. They differ on the meaning of "soon": Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi take it to mean while one is still in good health, before illness; al-Dahhak and Abu Mijlaz say before seeing the Angel of Death; Ikrima and Ibn Zayd say any time before death. A hadith transmitted by Abu Ayyub and others, that God accepts a servant's repentance so long as he has not begun the death rattle, is cited by several scholars. The second part of the verse, which denies repentance at the moment of death and to one who dies in disbelief, is understood by most as an absolute exclusion, while Abu al-Aliya reads the first part as addressed to believers and the second to hypocrites. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari discuss the nature of the divine commitment: most treat it as a promise grounded in generosity rather than an obligation. On whether acceptance is certain or only probable, al-Ash'ari, al-Ghazali and al-Razi hold it is certain, while al-Juwayni regards it as probable.

This verse says that repentance is not accepted from those who keep persisting in sins until death comes and they say, "Now I repent," nor from those who die in disbelief. Al-Tabari explains that "when death comes" refers to the death rattle and the sight of the angels coming to take the soul, when repentance is compelled rather than chosen. Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Zayd and Ibn 'Abbas are cited saying that repentance stays open as long as the soul has not reached the throat. The commentators agree that repentance is accepted before that stage, and that someone who dies as a disbeliever has no repentance. They differ on who the doers of evil are: Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima say they are polytheists, Abu al-'Aliya and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say they are hypocrites, while Sufyan al-Thawri and most exegetes speak of sinning Muslims, the view al-Tabari favours. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that "ignorance" in the verse means any act of disobedience, that is ignorance in acting rather than ignorance of the ruling, and they cite several Companions to this effect. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the verse covers both sinners and disbelievers. Ibn 'Atiyya presents the acceptance of sincere repentance as a strong likelihood for some scholars and as a certainty for others. On the word a'tadna, Abu 'Ubayda takes it to mean "we prepared," and the Kufan grammarians consider it synonymous with a'addna.

This verse abolishes a Jahiliyya custom that treated women as inheritance. It forbids inheriting women against their will: when a man died, his relatives could take his widow without a new dower, marry her to someone else and keep her dower, or confine her until she ransomed herself. The most cited occasion of revelation is the case of Kubayshah bint Ma'n after the death of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat. Commentators differ on the meaning of inheritance: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir mainly take it as inheriting the marriage, while others understand it as inheriting the women's property. The prohibition of confining a woman to force her to buy her freedom is addressed by most to husbands who dislike their wives, while Ibn Zayd and Mujahid address it to guardians. The exception of a manifest immorality (fahisha mubayyina) was explained by Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak as disobedience and ill conduct, whereas al-Hasan took it to mean adultery; al-Tabari holds that it covers any clear misconduct. All agree that wives must be treated kindly. Concerning dislike, the commentators note that it should not lead to hasty separation, for God may place much good in it, such as a righteous child or a change of heart. The verse about the qintar, the large sum given as dower, has been read in opposite ways: some take it as permitting a high dower, others as a mere image of abundance. They agree, however, that a husband may not take back what he gave once the marriage has been consummated.

This verse forbids a husband who divorces his wife in order to marry another from taking back anything of the dowry he has given her, even if it was a great amount. Al-Tabari explains that he must not harm the wife so that she ransoms herself with what she received, and Mujahid agrees, as Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report. The word bohtan is explained as injustice by Ibn Abbas and Ibn Qutayba, as falsehood by al-Zajjaj, and al-Razi defines it as a lie that bewilders the one it is told about. To justify the prohibition, most commentators cite the phrase how could you take it when you have been intimate with one another. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Sudi understand this as sexual union, while Abu Hanifa, as Ibn al-Jawzi notes, speaks of being alone together. All agree that the solemn covenant is the marriage contract, though some relate it to the husband's formula or to children. On the ruling, Bakr al-Muzani holds the verse absolute even in khul', while Ibn Zayd considers it abrogated by the verse in al-Baqara. Al-Tabari and most scholars consider it valid, with ransom still allowed in cases of discord or clear misconduct. The verse is also cited regarding the size of dowries: Umar wanted to limit them, then retracted when a woman quoted this verse to him. Commentators generally allow large dowries while recommending moderation.

The verse rebukes a man who would take back from his wife the bridal gift he gave her after having been intimate with her. The commentators explain that the word 'ifda' here means sexual intercourse, although Abu Hanifa, as reported by al-Razi and al-Nasafi, holds that valid seclusion suffices, and al-Farra' also takes this view. The 'solemn covenant' is understood in several ways: al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi take it to be the guardian's words at the contract, committing the husband to keep her with kindness or release her with goodness; Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take it to be the marriage formula by which intimacy becomes lawful; al-Sha'bi, 'Ikrima and al-Rabi' take it to be the Prophet's saying that you took them by God's trust and made their private parts lawful by God's word. Al-Zamakhshari reads it as the right of companionship and intimacy. Scholars differ on the ruling about a wife who asks for separation: Bakr al-Muzani held it firm without exception, while Ibn Zayd held it abrogated by the verse of al-Baqara; al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya held it firm and not abrogated, limiting the prohibition to a husband who wishes to replace his wife without any fault on her part. As for the phrase 'a qintar', some read it as hyperbole and others as a permission; 'Umar forbade excessive dowries and then retracted after a woman challenged him with this verse. The overall sense is that taking back the dowry after the marriage is forbidden, and that returning it is a matter of justice and kindness between spouses.

This verse forbids sons from marrying the wives their fathers have married. The commentators explain that some pre-Islamic Arabs practised this, and the occasion-of-revelation reports name Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat and others who did so. The verse calls it an abomination, something hateful to God and to people of honour, and an evil path. The phrase 'except what has passed' is understood by most as a disconnected exception meaning 'but what is past': what was done before the prohibition is forgiven. Al-Tabari takes 'ma' to refer to the act, a marriage of that kind, while Ibn Abbas and most exegetes take it to refer to the women, so the marriage contract alone makes a woman forbidden to the son, even without consummation. Ibn Zayd reads the verb as sexual intercourse and extends the ban to illicit unions. Al-Razi reviews the legal debate over whether nikah means the contract or the act. Scholars also disagree on whether a woman a father fornicated with becomes forbidden to his son: Abu Hanifa says yes and al-Shafi'i says no. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith in which the Prophet sends a man to execute someone who married his father's wife, which some use to justify severe punishment. The commentators agree that the three descriptions, fahisha, maqt and sa'a sabila, rank the offence as extremely grave.

This verse lists the women forbidden in marriage, either permanently or for a time. Seven are forbidden by blood: mothers, daughters, sisters, paternal and maternal aunts, nieces through a brother, and nieces through a sister. Mothers include grandmothers, and daughters include granddaughters however distant. Milk relations make unlawful what blood relations do, so the nursing mother and milk sisters are forbidden; most scholars, following the Prophetic tradition, fix this at five known feedings within the two years of nursing. By marriage, the wife's mother becomes forbidden as soon as the contract is concluded, whereas the wife's daughter is forbidden only once the marriage has been consummated with the mother. Wives of one's own sons are forbidden, but not wives of adopted sons. Two sisters may not be combined in marriage, nor a woman with her paternal aunt or maternal aunt, as the Prophet taught. What was done before Islam is forgiven, for God is Forgiving and Merciful. Scholars differ on some details: the majority holds that living in the stepfather's household is not a condition for the prohibition of a stepdaughter, while Dawud and the Zahiris require it; they also debate whether the consummation that creates the prohibition includes touching or looking with desire, whether adult nursing counts, whether the father's milk creates kinship, and whether two sisters held as slave-concubines may be combined, which some allow and most forbid.

The verse forbids marrying women who already have husbands, except those whom your right hands possess through captivity in war, who become lawful after being purified by a period of waiting. It makes lawful everything beyond the listed prohibitions, on condition that one seeks marriage with one's wealth in chastity rather than fornication. It requires giving the full dowry to those one has enjoyed, and says there is no blame in what the spouses agree between them after the dowry is fixed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most commentators understand the muhsanat as married women, and link the exception to the captives of Awtas, as reported by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. Some transmitted reports from Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Jabir and Ibn Abbas held that selling a married slave-girl divorces her, but the majority rejected this, citing the case of Barira, whom the Prophet allowed to choose. Others understand the muhsanat as chaste or free women, and see the verse as forbidding adultery. Commentators also differ on temporary marriage, mut'a: most hold it was permitted and then abrogated, while Ibn Abbas and some companions allowed it in cases of necessity. Some link the end of the verse to the amount of the dowry, others to mutual agreement on a reduction or increase, the reading favoured by al-Tabari.

This verse concerns marrying believing slave women for one who cannot afford to marry a free believing woman and fears falling into fornication. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, take tawl to mean wealth, ample means and the ability to pay the dowry. Rabi'a, al-Nakha'i, Qatada and 'Ata' understand it as patience and self-restraint for a man who has become so attached to one slave-girl that he cannot desire another. Abu Hanifa holds that tawl means having a free wife, so that the man is then forbidden to marry a slave. All agree that the slave must be a believer, that outward faith suffices since God knows hearts, and many require the masters' permission, a proper dowry, and chastity, meaning neither open immorality nor secret lovers. On the phrase about being married, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it to mean marriage, while Ibn Mas'ud and al-Sha'bi take it to mean Islam. They agree that a married slave-woman receives half the punishment of a free woman, fifty lashes, since stoning cannot be halved. Opinions differ on the unmarried slave. Most understand the anxiety of falling into sin as the hardship meant, and consider patience better, since a slave's children follow their mother into slavery.

This verse says that God wishes to make clear to the believers the rules of their religion and what serves their affairs, to guide them along the paths of the righteous who came before them, among the prophets and their followers, and to turn them back from disobedience to obedience. The commentators largely agree that this clarification concerns what is lawful and unlawful in marriage and the forbidden degrees, and that being guided to the ways of earlier communities means following the rightly guided among them. The grammarians differ over the lam in 'li-yubayyina': Sibawayh and most Basran grammarians take it as a lam of purpose with an implied object, while al-Farra' and the Kufans take it as equivalent to 'an', which al-Tabari adopts; al-Zamakhshari regards it as an emphatic lam. As for 'the ways of those before you', al-Kalbi and al-Baghawi identify them with the prohibition of mothers, daughters and sisters that already bound earlier peoples, others with the upright religion of Abraham, and al-Nasafi and al-Zamakhshari with the conduct of the prophets and the righteous. Regarding God's turning in mercy, many take it as the servant's return from sin to obedience or as God enabling that return, while al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya understand it as forgiveness and the erasing of past faults. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that this guidance may consist in the uniformity of the laws in obedience and hearing, and al-Razi holds that the laws differ in themselves but agree in their benefits. The next verse develops the theme: God wishes to turn to you in forgiveness, while those who follow their desires wish you to deviate far; Mujahid identifies them with fornicators, as-Suddi with Jews and Christians, and Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari with anyone pursuing a forbidden desire.

This verse says that God wishes to turn towards His servants and forgive their past sins, while those who follow their desires wish that the believers swerve from the truth into a tremendous deviation. The commentators agree on the general meaning: it is a warning against turning away from God's law in pursuit of pleasures. They differ, however, on who "those who follow their desires" are. Mujahid, followed by Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Jaza'iri, identifies them as fornicators; as-Suddi names the Jews and Christians; Ibn Zayd includes anyone who follows a forbidden desire, and al-Tabari favours this broad reading because it covers all cases. Some, such as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan, report that the reference is to the Jews, who wanted the Muslims to marry their paternal sisters, and others mention the Magians, who permitted the same.

The commentators also agree that God's willing here is a prescriptive will, a sign of mercy, and that the repetition of "God desires to turn to you" serves to emphasise and to prepare the mention of the passionate people's wish. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that the deviation is departure from the truth through disobedience, and that it is called tremendous in comparison with an isolated lapse. As for the next phrase, "God wants to lighten your burden, for man was created weak", Mujahid, Tawus and Ibn Zayd explain it as the permission to marry believing slave women, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir extend it to the easing of the obligations generally; Ibn 'Atiyya treats the first meaning as the immediate purpose and the second as a wider scope.

The commentators explain that God, by what He prescribes in this verse, intends to lighten the burden on the believers, because man was created weak, unable to hold out long against his desires or to bear fully the hardships of obedience. They differ on the scope of this lightening. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, Tawus and Muqatil take it mainly as the permission to marry believing slave women when one cannot afford a free woman and fears sin, understanding human weakness as the difficulty of restraining oneself before women; Ibn al-Musayyab, cited by several, stressed the strength of the temptation women represent. Ibn Zayd and most exegetes, however, hold that the verse covers all the rulings of the Law: the religion was made easy and not made heavy as it was for the Children of Israel, and they support this with verses saying that God wants ease for you. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report that for many the weakness means the weakness of the inclination to obedience in the face of the many calls of desire, while al-Hasan understood it as weakness of constitution, since man was created from a despised water; most did not adopt this reading. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that this lightening includes everything God has made easy for His servants, and that the verse comes in the manner of grace. Ibn 'Abbas counted this verse among the eight verses of Surat al-Nisa' that he considered better for this community than all that the sun rises upon, according to a report given by al-Tabari. Overall, the commentators see in this verse a conclusion that introduces the earlier marriage rulings and reminds that the Law rests on ease and mercy, human weakness being one of the reasons for that indulgence.

This verse forbids believers to consume one another's property wrongfully, meaning by any means the law does not allow, such as usury, gambling, seizure, theft or breach of trust, and it makes an exception for trade concluded by mutual consent. Commentators differ on what consent requires. Al-Tabari, with al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and most of the early scholars, holds that the parties keep the option to withdraw until they physically separate, citing the hadith that the two sellers have the choice as long as they have not parted. Malik and Abu Hanifa hold that the sale is complete once offer and acceptance are exchanged, without any requirement of separation, a view also reflected in Ibn Atiyya and al-Nasafi. Al-Razi reads the verse as covering any transaction the sharia does not sanction, while al-Qurtubi argues that physical separation is not required. The Kufan readers recite the word tijaratan in the accusative, the others in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari understands consent as the agreement of the parties at the moment of contracting. As for 'do not kill yourselves', al-Hasan and al-Sudi take it to forbid killing one another, since believers are like a single soul, while others take it to forbid suicide or exposing oneself to ruin. 'Amr ibn al-'As relied on it to justify dry ablution in severe cold, and the Prophet did not reprove him. The verse threatens with the Fire whoever does this out of aggression and wrongdoing, and Ibn Kathir concludes from it that suicide is among the major sins.

This verse warns that whoever does what is forbidden, namely killing a soul or consuming others' wealth unjustly, out of transgression and wrongdoing, will be cast into the Fire, and that this is easy for God. The commentators differ on what "that" refers to. 'Ata', al-Zajjaj and al-Qurtubi take it to mean killing, or killing together with the consumption of wealth, while Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir extend it to everything forbidden since the beginning of the surah. Al-Tabari chooses a middle position, the prohibitions that come before this verse, since each of them is linked to a threat. On the two words "transgression" and "wrongdoing", most scholars distinguish them: transgression is going beyond limits, wrongdoing is putting a thing in the wrong place. Others treat them as synonyms used for emphasis, and al-Baydawi says that transgression concerns others while wrongdoing concerns oneself by exposing oneself to punishment. On the phrase about burning, Ibn Kathir cites many hadiths about the fate of one who takes his own life, and he reports the scholars' disagreement about the major sins: Ibn 'Abbas defines them as whatever is threatened with the Fire, while Ibn Mas'ud limits them to the prohibitions of the surah up to the thirtieth verse, and others give different lists.

This part of the verse promises believers that God will expiate their minor sins and admit them to an honourable abode if they avoid the major sins they have been forbidden. The plain meaning is that deliberately refraining from grave sins is the way to having lesser ones erased and to attaining the abode of honour. The commentators agree that sins divide into major and minor, that minor ones are expiated by avoiding major ones, and that the five prayers, Friday prayer and Ramadan fasting expiate what lies between them when major sins are avoided, as the hadith states. On defining a major sin, however, they differ. Ibn Mas'ud ties it to the prohibitions stated earlier in the sura, Ali and Ubayd ibn Umayr count seven, Ibn Umar counts nine, and Ibn Mas'ud in another report counts four. Ibn Abbas defines it as any sin threatened with fire, curse or wrath, while others hold that whatever God forbids is grave. Al-Juwayni, al-Isfara'ini and al-Qushayri argued that all sins are grave and only relative comparison makes some small, whereas al-Razi and Ibn Hazm took other lines. Most scholars hold that a grave sin is one carrying a legal penalty in this world or a threat in the next. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari also report that Umar ibn al-Khattab cited this verse to Egyptians who demanded that rulings be enforced which they could not fully keep themselves.

This verse forbids wishing for what God has given some of you over others, whether wealth, status, knowledge or anything else, since this distribution comes from His wisdom and His knowledge of what suits each person. Many commentators report that the occasion of revelation was Umm Salama's words: men fight and women do not, and women receive only half the inheritance. Others say that women wished for equal reward with men, while men hoped for a greater reward in the Hereafter as they have a greater share of inheritance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi emphasise the general scope of the verse, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others take 'share' to mean inheritance, and Qatada takes it to mean the reward and punishment for deeds. All agree that envy and wishing a blessing removed from others is forbidden. Al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya regard wishing for another's possessions as prohibited, whereas the majority allow wishing for a similar blessing without desiring its loss, citing the hadith that there is no envy except in two cases. On what to ask, some understand it as asking God for His bounty in general, others as asking for worship, and Ibn Sa'di says one should ask for what benefits both religion and worldly life. Ibn Sa'di and others note that God does not command asking except to give, and the verse closes by reminding that God knows all things.

This verse establishes that God has appointed for each person, men and women alike, heirs who inherit what parents and close relatives leave behind. It then commands that those bound to you by an oath of alliance be given their share. The commentators agree that this refers to the pre-Islamic alliance, in which an ally could inherit, as Qatada and al-Zamakhshari explain through formulas such as 'my blood is your blood, you inherit from me and I from you'. They differ on what this means now. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and most early scholars hold that it was abrogated by the verse 'blood relatives are closer to one another in the Book of God' (al-Anfal 75), so inheritance passed to kinsmen. Mujahid, Ibrahim, Ata, al-SudDi and, in another report, Ibn Abbas understand the share as support, aid and assistance without inheritance, so the verse stands. Abu Hanifa holds that the ally inherits when there is no other heir, while al-Shafi'i and Malik deny this and assign such estates to the Muslim community. Ibn Kathir leans toward abrogation, while al-Tabari takes the sense of mutual support, citing the hadith that Islam allows no new alliance but only strengthened older ones. The verse closes by stating that God is a witness over all things, and so knows what is given and what is withheld.

This verse states that men are the guardians and maintainers of women, because God has given some of them an advantage over others and because they spend from their wealth, namely the dower and maintenance. The commentators explain that righteous women are obedient to God and to their husbands, and guard what is entrusted to them in their husbands' absence, by God's guidance. As for those whose rebellion is feared, they are first admonished, then left apart in the bed, then struck in a way that does not cause injury. If they obey, no pretext should be sought against them, and God is the Most High, the Great, who warns against arrogance toward them.

The commentators agree that qawama means authority, protection and management, that obedience is expected in what is proper, and that the remedy follows a sequence: admonition, then separation in bed, then striking. They differ on the meaning of separation: Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr understood it as abstaining from intercourse while still sharing the bed; al-Dahhak and al-Suddi as ceasing speech and turning the back; 'Ikrima and al-Hasan as harsh speech; al-Tabari proposed binding the wife, a view criticised by Ibn al-'Arabi and al-Qurtubi. They also differ on whether striking may be used as soon as rebellion appears: al-Shafi'i allowed it, while others required the sequence to be followed.

The reports about the occasion of revelation speak of an Ansari man who slapped his wife, after which she sought retaliation; some of these reports are considered weak, and al-Tabari regarded the account as probably mursal.

The next verse provides that if discord between spouses is feared, two arbiters are appointed, one from each family, who seek reconciliation, and God will grant accord. The scholars differ over their powers: some see them as agents acting on the mandate of the spouses, others as judges able to decree separation or compensation, and others as conciliators who may testify against the wrongdoer without the power to dissolve the marriage.

This verse teaches that when discord between spouses grows so severe that each stands on opposite sides, the ruler or those in authority should send two just arbiters, one from the husband's family and one from the wife's, to investigate the situation and work toward reconciliation. If reconciliation proves impossible, they may separate the couple after establishing which party is at fault. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi report the majority view that the arbiters are appointed by the judge and may rule even without the spouses' consent. Al-Hasan and Qatada hold that they may reunite the couple but not separate them. Abu Hanifa, and one of al-Shafi'i's opinions, treat the arbiters as agents whose ruling needs the spouses' approval, relying on 'Ali's words to the husband: 'You lie, until you admit what she has admitted.' According to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak, the pronoun in 'if they desire reconciliation' refers to the arbiters themselves, while the pronoun in 'between them' generally refers to the spouses, though other readings exist. The commentators agree that shiqaq means discord and enmity, and al-Razi and al-Baghawi explain that the word 'fear' may mean knowledge or suspicion. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-'Arabi note disagreement over whether a single arbiter suffices or whether non-relatives may serve. The verse closes by mentioning God's knowledge and awareness, reassuring those who sincerely seek reconciliation that God will grant them success.

The verse commands worship of God alone, without any partner, and kindness to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the near and distant neighbour, the companion at one's side, the traveller, and those whom one's right hand possesses. The commentators agree that worship covers every act of obedience to God and that the prohibition of association applies to all its forms. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the Qur'an often joins worship of God with kindness to parents, and that closer relatives take precedence. On the near neighbour, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean a blood relative, while Nawf al-Shami understands the Muslim neighbour and the distant neighbour as the non-Muslim, and others measure nearness by the distance between homes. On the companion at the side, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say it is the fellow traveller, 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud say the wife, and Ibn Zayd says the one who stays close hoping for your benefit. On the wayfarer, Mujahid says the passer-by, al-Dahhak and al-Shafi'i the one in need, and most commentators the guest. The verse closes by stating that God does not love the arrogant and the boastful, since these traits lead a person to neglect these duties. The commentators cite numerous traditions on the neighbour and the servant, including the duty to feed and clothe those under one's authority as one feeds and clothes oneself, and not to burden them with what they cannot bear.

This verse states that Allah does not love the arrogant and boastful, then describes those who are miserly, who urge others to be miserly, and who conceal what Allah has given them of His bounty, promising a humiliating punishment to the disbelievers. The commentators differ on what this miserliness refers to. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Razi report that it means the Jews who hid the description of the Prophet ﷺ found in the Torah, a view transmitted from Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi. Al-Tabari, Ibn Ishaq and al-Wahidi also report, through Ibn 'Abbas, that some Jewish scholars told the Ansar not to spend their wealth for fear of poverty, so the miserliness concerns money. Sa'id ibn Jubayr took it to mean withholding knowledge. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya consider that it means refusing to spend in obedience to God. Al-Tabari prefers concealing knowledge, since no nation has ever commanded miserliness as a religious virtue, while al-Razi holds that the wording covers both miserliness with knowledge and with wealth. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan discuss its grammatical role as an apposition, an object of blame, or a subject with an implied predicate. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin extend the meaning to withholding anything that is obligatory to give, whether money, knowledge, status or effort. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read bil-bakhal, while most readers recite bil-bukhl, both forms being accepted with the same meaning. Al-Tabari explains the humiliating punishment as a degrading retribution.

This part of the verse describes people who spend their wealth to be seen by others, not seeking the face of God, and who believe neither in God nor in the Last Day. It then says that whoever takes Satan as a companion has an evil companion. The commentators explain that this spending lacks true faith and has only an outward appearance. Most of them, including al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi, hold that the verse refers to the hypocrites, who displayed Islam out of caution while remaining unbelievers; they rely on the mention of showing off, which they link to double-dealing.

Mujahid, as reported by al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya, applies the verse to the Jews, and al-Tabari rejects this because the Jews did believe in God and the Last Day. Ibn 'Atiyya replies that their faith is of no benefit, so it is as good as none. Others, such as al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur, point to the pagans of Mecca who spent against the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn 'Abbas also reports a context in which Jews discouraged the Ansar from spending.

As for Satan, most exegetes understand him as the one who accompanies such people and drives them to act this way, as al-Nasafi states. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi note that the phrase may also be a warning that Satan will be bound to them in the Fire. On the word qarin, al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi take it to mean a close companion. On the grammar of 'fa-saa qarinan', Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur treat qarinan as a specifier (tamyiz), while others take it as a circumstantial or detached accusative.

This verse asks, in a tone of reproach, what harm would come to them if they believed in God and the Last Day and spent from what God had provided. The commentators explain that faith and giving in God's path carry no harm at all, and that the real loss lies in their present condition. Most read the question as a rebuke intended to make them see what benefits them, not as a genuine enquiry. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi compare it to saying to an undutiful son: what would it cost you to be dutiful? The closing words, 'and God is ever Knowing of them', are taken as a warning that God knows their hidden intentions.

The commentators disagree on who is meant. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir apply the verse to the hypocrites who spend to be seen, while Mujahid says it refers to the Jews, a view al-Tabari judges weak because the people described do not believe in God or the Last Day. Al-Wahidi and Ibn Atiyya also mention the pagans of Mecca, and Ibn Atiyya suggests Mujahid's view can be read as hyperbole. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi raise a theological debate: the Mu'tazilites argue from the verse that humans can choose faith, since no one is asked to do what they cannot, while the Sunni scholars reply that humans acquire the act while God alone creates it.

All agree on one point: giving has value only when it is sincere and done for God's sake. Ibn Kathir links the verse to stinginess and to hiding the favours one has received, while others see it as refusal to give to relatives and the poor.
placeholder

The commentators explain that the verse describes the state of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, when God will bring a witness from every community, its prophet, and will bring Muhammad ﷺ as a witness over his own people. They differ on the nature of this testimony. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Juraij, al-Suddi and Muqatil hold that the prophets testify that they delivered their Lord's message, while Mujahid and Qatada say they testify to the deeds of their peoples. Abu al-'Aliya understands it as testimony to their faith, and al-Zajjaj as testimony both for and against. As for the word 'these', some apply it to the Quraysh and other disbelievers, others to the community of Muhammad ﷺ; al-Tabari and al-Qasimi say he testifies to its truthfulness and against its denial. All agree on the report from Ibn Mas'ud, in which the Prophet wept on hearing the verse and said 'Enough'. Some add that the witness covers those he saw and those he did not see. The following verse continues the scene: the disbelievers wish the earth would swallow them and cannot hide anything from God. Ibn 'Abbas explains that they first deny their polytheism and then their limbs bear witness against them, while al-Razi and others present alternatives, either as a separate scene or as a separate statement, since their deeds are manifest to God.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when God brings a witness from every community. Those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were levelled over them, that they might be swallowed up or turned to dust like it, and they will be unable to hide anything from God. The commentators agree on the core meaning: this is a wish to vanish in order to escape shame and punishment. They differ on the verb tusawwa. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Abu 'Ubayda say the earth will split open and they will sink into it, while al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan understand that they will become dust like the earth. The recitations differ: Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read the passive form, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read with an initial ta and a doubled sin, and Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with an initial ta and a single sin. On the phrase they cannot hide anything from God, Ibn 'Abbas explains that their limbs will testify after their mouths are sealed. Al-Hasan holds that the Day has several stations, in some of which they deny and swear and in others they confess. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy report that some read the clause as an independent statement, since their deeds are plain to God. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a description of their state of fear.

This verse concerns two rulings about prayer. Commentators report that it was revealed while wine was still permitted: Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf hosted companions who drank until intoxicated, and one of them led the evening prayer and garbled his recitation. The apparent meaning is that believers must not approach prayer while intoxicated, until they regain their senses and know what they are saying. Most exegetes take intoxication to mean wine, though al-Dahhak understood drowsiness, and al-Tabari favoured wine. All agree that one in a state of major impurity (junub) must not pray until he washes. On the exception 'except passers-by', Ali, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Farra and al-Zajjaj took it to mean the traveller without water who performs tayammum, while Ibn Masud, Said ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i and al-Zuhri took it to mean one crossing the mosque without staying. Al-Shafi'i permitted the junub to cross the mosque; Abu Hanifa limited this to cases where there is water or a passage. The sick whom water would harm, the traveller, one who has relieved himself or is in major impurity may perform tayammum; scholars disagreed about a resident who finds no water: Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and Muhammad permitted it, Abu Yusuf and Zufar did not. Tayammum is with clean earth, understood by most as the surface of the ground, while al-Shafi'i required dust clinging to the hand; most prescribe one strike for face and hands. On the meaning of touching women, Ali, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatada took it as intercourse, while Ibn Masud, Ibn Umar and al-Sha'bi took it as skin contact, the view of al-Shafi'i; al-Tabari preferred intercourse. The verse closes by affirming that God is pardoning and forgiving, who eases the burden of His servants.

This verse marvels at people who were given a share of the Scripture yet chose misguidance over guidance, denying the signs of the Prophet ﷺ and remaining in Judaism after the proof was clear, while wishing that the believers would also stray from the right path. The commentators read it as a warning: the believers should not seek counsel from the enemies of Islam, since God knows their hostility best, and God is sufficient as protector and helper. On the meaning of buying misguidance, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari take it as preferring error to guidance, al-Zajjaj as taking bribes to keep their leadership, and Ibn Atiyya reports that some gave money to their rabbis to reject the Prophet. On the phrase 'of those who judaized', Ibn Atiyya offers several readings, while Sibawayh sees an omitted word. On distorting the words, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid describe it as misinterpreting the Book, while al-Tabari includes changing the wording or the meaning. Several commentators report that the word 'ra'ina' was addressed to the Prophet intending insult, and that the believers were forbidden to use it. As for believing only a little, most take it to mean a faith that does not benefit them, while others apply it to particular individuals such as Abdullah ibn Salam.

In this verse God tells the believers that He knows their enemies better than they do, and that God suffices as a protector who takes charge of their affairs and as a helper who defends them. They should therefore not turn to their enemies or seek support from anyone other than Him. The context concerns the Jews who had been given a share of the Torah yet chose misguidance in exchange for guidance and wanted the believers to stray from the path. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi agree that the primary target is the Jewish scholars and rabbis, and the warning is that believers should not seek counsel from those hostile to their faith. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God's knowledge covers the hatred and envy hidden in their hearts. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the form 'a'lam may be a comparative, while others read it as meaning 'knowing'. On the particle 'bi' in 'bi-Allah', al-Zajjaj takes it as carrying the sense of a command, 'be content with God', whereas most grammarians, including Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan, regard it as a redundant particle added for emphasis. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir relate the occasion of revelation transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas about Rifa'a ibn Zayd, who twisted his tongue when saying 'ra'ina', but this account illuminates the context rather than fixing the verse's meaning. The commentators agree that the verse promises sufficiency and support to the believers and carries a warning to their enemies, protection and help belonging to God alone.

This verse describes a group of Jews who distorted God's words from their proper places. Mujahid explains this as altering the Torah, while Ibn Abbas reports that they twisted the Prophet's words after leaving his presence. They said to the Prophet, "We hear and we disobey" and "Hear, without being heard," which Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd understand as "may you not hear," whereas al-Hasan and Mujahid take it to mean "unaccepted from you"; al-Tabari favours the first reading. The word "ra'ina" looks like a request to attend to us, but they meant something like "fool," twisting it with their tongues, which al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi see as mockery of the religion. The commentators note that the proper words would have been "we hear and obey" and "look at us," which would have been better and more upright for them. God cursed them for their disbelief, so they believe only a little. On the meaning of "little," Ibn Abbas, Muqatil and Ibn Kathir refer to a small group such as Abdullah ibn Salam, while Qatada and al-Zajjaj take it to mean a weak faith of no benefit. Al-Zamakhshari allows that it may mean no faith at all.

This verse addresses the People of the Book, chiefly the Jews, urging them to believe in the Qur'an, which confirms what they already possess of the Torah, and warning them that refusal will bring punishment: their faces may be obliterated and turned backward, or they may be cursed as the people of the Sabbath were. The commentators differ on the meaning of obliteration. Ibn Abbas, al-Awfi and Qatada took it as blinding, with eyes set at the back of the head so that people walk backwards; Ibn Abbas also explained it as erasing the features until faces resemble the nape. Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak understood a spiritual loss, turning hearts away from guidance toward error. Ibn Zayd read it as the expulsion of the Jews from their homes and their return to Syria, while al-Farra' suggested faces covered with hair like those of monkeys. Al-Tabari reports that the threat was not carried out because some of them believed, and he preferred a physical reading. Al-Mubarrad held that the threat still awaits fulfilment before the Last Day, while others held it was conditional on unbelief. For the curse, most identify it with transformation into apes, while Ibn Atiyya took it as humiliation. All agree that God's command is carried out. Several report that Abdallah ibn Salam and Ka'b al-Ahbar converted out of fear of this warning, and that the verse was revealed concerning rabbis who denied knowing the truth of the Prophet.

The commentators explain that this verse states God does not forgive associating partners with Him, while He may forgive lesser sins to whomever He wills, and that whoever associates others with God has invented an enormous sin. Al-Tabari reports that it was revealed after a question put to the Prophet about shirk following the verse of Az-Zumar, while Mujahid and others read it as a warning against idolatry. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi emphasise that shirk is not forgiven without repentance and that one should not despair of God's mercy. The Mu'tazilites tie forgiveness to repentance and read God's will as applying to the penitent, whereas the Murji'ites relate the will to faith. Al-Razi considers the verse one of the strongest proofs for pardoning grave sins, and Ibn Juzayy regards it as the decisive text on punishment. Ibn 'Atiyya presents the Sunni position: a believer who sins is under God's will, who may punish him and then admit him to Paradise, or pardon him at once. The commentators set out these views without judging between them.

The verse rebukes those who praise themselves and claim purity, and affirms that true purification belongs to God alone, who purifies whom He wills, without anyone being wronged even by a fatil. The commentators agree that the Jews are meant, but differ on how they justified themselves. Qatada and al-Hasan take it to be their claim to be the sons and beloved of God and that Paradise is theirs alone. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi read it as their claim to be free of sin like their children. Mujahid, Ikrima and Abu Malik report that they had their young children lead the prayer, believing the children sinless. Ibn Abbas reports that they claimed their deceased children would intercede for them, and Ibn Mas'ud took it as their mutual praise of one another. Al-Tabari prefers the first view as the most apparent, holding that the explanation about leading prayer needs a sound report. On the fatil, Ibn Abbas, Ata' and Mujahid say it is the thread in the middle of the date stone, while al-Suddi and Abu Malik say it is the dirt rolled out between the fingers; all these meanings point to something extremely small. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith against excessive praise of a person, and al-Qurtubi and al-Razi stress that real praise comes from God. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note, however, that the Prophet was not covered by this prohibition, since God had already praised him. The next verse turns to the People of the Book who believe in jibt and taghut.

The verse tells the Prophet to marvel at those, mainly Jews (some commentators also include Christians), who praise themselves and claim purity and closeness to God, thereby fabricating a lie against Him; this sin alone is enough to make them plainly guilty. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree that the Jews are meant, though they differ on the form of this self-praise. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it to be their claim to be God's sons and beloved, and their saying that only Jews or Christians enter Paradise. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi take it to be their claim to be free of sin, that what they do by day is expiated by night and vice versa. Mujahid, Ikrima and Abu Malik take it to be placing their children at the front of prayer, believing them sinless. Ibn Abbas takes it to be their belief that their dead ancestors will intercede for them, and Ibn Mas'ud their mutual praise. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir stress that only the purification granted by God counts, and that the principle applies to anyone who praises himself. The word fatil is, for most, the thread in the cleft of a date stone, and for others the dirt rolled out between the fingers; both images express utter insignificance. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi specify that the lie lies in their claim to be pure before God.

This verse marvels at certain People of the Book who were given a share of revelation yet believe in al-jibt and al-taghut and tell the disbelievers that they are better guided than the believers. The commentators agree that the reference is to a group of Jews, most likely of Medina, but differ on the meaning of the two words. Ikrima says they are two idols worshipped by the Quraysh; 'Umar, Abu al-'Aliya, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada say jibt is magic or the sorcerer and taghut is the devil or the soothsayer; Ibn 'Abbas, in one report, says jibt is the idols and taghut their custodians who dress up worship to mislead people. Al-Dahhak identifies them with Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. Al-Tabari concludes that both words cover anything worshipped or obeyed apart from God, a view also given by Malik and al-Zajjaj. The reported occasion of revelation is that Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Huyayy ibn Akhtab went to Mecca after Uhud to ally with the Quraysh against the Prophet, and when the Quraysh asked which religion was better, they favoured the polytheists; the reports differ on the exact speakers. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the verse as a curse on them and a statement that they will have no helper. Al-Razi sees deliberate obstinacy here. Some commentators read the following verses as a rebuke of the envy and stinginess these Jews showed towards the Prophet and the believers.

This verse states that those given a portion of the Book, understood by most commentators as Jews, have been cast away from God's mercy and cursed for believing in jibt and taghut and for telling the disbelievers that they were better guided than the believers; whoever God curses will have no helper to protect him from punishment. The commentators agree that the verse concerns a group of Jews, and that cursing means being removed from mercy and abandoned. On the meaning of jibt and taghut, opinions differ: Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Aliya take jibt as the Abyssinian word for sorcerer and taghut as the soothsayer; Umar and Ibn Mas'ud take them as sorcery and Satan; Ikrima and al-Dahhak identify them as two idols or as the Jewish leaders Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf; and Abu Ubayda and Malik define taghut as anything worshipped besides God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi relate the occasion of revelation: after Uhud, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions went to Mecca to ally with the Quraysh against the Prophet, and when the Quraysh asked them which religion was better, they praised paganism. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi read the verse as a rebuke of envy and stubbornness, and al-Razi adds that preferring the worship of others to monotheism is plainly absurd. For the next verse, most commentators understand it as denying that the Jews have any share of dominion, since their stinginess would prevent them from giving even a speck such as the nuqayr, the mark on a date stone; Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari instead see the envy as directed at the Prophet and the believers for the favour God gave them.

This verse, in the view of most commentators, denies that the Jews have any share of dominion, and then states that if they had any, they would not give people even the smallest thing. The word naqir is explained by Ibn Abbas, Ata', al-Dahhak and Qatada as the small pit on the back of the date stone from which the palm grows, a image of utmost smallness; Mujahid takes it to be the seed at the centre of the stone, while Abu al-Aliya reports a gesture of pressing the thumb on a finger. Al-Tabari prefers the smallest such pit, all the opinions conveying littleness. As for dominion, Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di understand it as authority and power over affairs, al-Razi mentions prophethood or wealth, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi refer to worldly kingship or the kingship of God. According to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ikrima, the following verses concern the Prophet alone, whose distinction is prophethood or the permission to have several wives, whereas Qatada takes the people to mean the Arabs. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir note that the family of Abraham was given the Book, wisdom and a great kingdom, and that among them some believed while others turned away. Grammarians debate the particle 'idhan': Sibawayh regards it as non-governing after the fa, while some readings with the verb in the subjunctive treat it as governing.

In this verse God rebukes the Jews for envying the people for the favours He has given them, reminding them that He gave the family of Abraham the Book, wisdom and a great kingdom, so there is no reason to be surprised that He grants a favour to Muhammad. The commentators agree that this envy is blameworthy, and the passage is read as part of a wider condemnation of both envy and stinginess. On who the "people" are, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak take it to mean the Prophet alone, Qatada takes it to mean the Arabs among whom he was sent, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir include the Prophet with his companions or the believers. As for the favour envied, Qatada, al-Hasan and al-Tabari understand prophethood, whereas Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi understand the permission to take several wives without limit; al-Tabari finds this second reading out of keeping with the praising tone of the passage. On the "great kingdom", most commentators, following Ibn 'Abbas, take it to be Solomon's rule, Mujahid takes it to be prophethood, and Hammam ibn al-Harith takes it to be support from the angels; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour Solomon's kingdom. The commentators also report that the Jews objected to the Prophet's many wives, and were told that David and Solomon had more. The following verses distinguish those who believed from those who turned away, and Hell suffices as punishment for the latter.

This verse says that the People of the Book divided over the revelation given to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: some believed in it and followed him, while others turned away and kept people from him, and the Fire of Hell is enough as their punishment. The commentators differ on what the pronoun "him" refers to. Most, including Mujahid, Muqatil, al-Farra' and Ibn Kathir, take it to mean the Qur'an or what was revealed to Muhammad, so the believers are those who accepted it, and Ibn Kathir specifies those who believed in Muhammad, such as Abdullah ibn Salam. Al-Tabari understands turning away as refusing to affirm it. Al-Suddi and Muqatil take the pronoun to refer to Abraham or to the Book, giving the sense that among Abraham's descendants some believed and some disbelieved, a view also noted by Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi. Al-Zamakhshari identifies those who denied his prophethood while knowing it was true. As for "sa'ir", al-Tabari explains it as a kindled fire, and Ibn 'Atiyya explains it as the intensity of the blaze, a figure of extreme torment. The commentators agree that the passage consoles the Prophet, since the division between peoples and their prophets is an old pattern.

This verse warns those who reject Allah's signs that they will be burned in the Fire. Whenever their skins are roasted through, Allah will replace them with new skins so that the punishment continues and is fully tasted. He is Mighty and Wise. The commentators agree that the pain falls on the conscious soul rather than the skin itself, and that the word for burning means roasting in fire. On how the skin is replaced, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that it is the same skin restored unburnt, the change being only in its form, like a ring melted down and reshaped. Al-Suddi and Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya hold that Allah creates entirely new skins, while some, cited by al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi, understand the skins to mean the garments of tar mentioned in Surah Ibrahim, a view Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya call weak because it departs from the plain meaning.
