Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan and others report that the renewal happens many times in a single hour or day, and that the skins become white like papyrus sheets. To the objection of how an unsinning skin can be punished, al-Razi replies that skin is not the essence of the human but an instrument, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi say the pain is felt by the soul. The passage then turns to the reward of believers: gardens with flowing rivers, purified spouses and deep shade, which Ibn Kathir and others take as a shade that never fades, and which is illustrated with the hadith about the tree of eternity.

This verse sets the promise to believers against the threat to disbelievers: God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow, to abide therein forever. They will have purified spouses, and God will shelter them in a dense, lasting shade. The commentators agree that faith and good works go together, and that the deeds must be sincere and in accordance with the law, as Ibn Kathir reports and Ibn 'Uthaymin stresses. They also agree that the abode is eternal and that the spouses are purified, free from physical impurities such as menstruation and from blameworthy traits, as Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir explain. The meaning of the 'dense shade' is disputed. Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and al-Hasan take it to be a shade where neither heat nor scorching wind reaches, while al-Dahhak understands it as the shade of trees and palaces, and al-Kalbi as lasting shade. Abu Muslim and others regard the phrase as mere emphasis, like the Arabic 'a very dark night'. Al-Tabari cites the hadith of the tree under which a rider could travel for a hundred years. Al-Razi reads the image as one of security and rest, since the Arabs held shade to be among the greatest comforts in their scorching land. The passage thus describes a lasting felicity combining pleasure and security, with variations of interpretation concerning the shade and the spouses.

This verse commands that trusts be returned to their rightful owners and that people be judged with justice when one rules between them. It calls this command an excellent admonition and ends by affirming that God hears and sees all. The commentators disagree about who is addressed and why it was revealed. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn Aslam, Shahr ibn Hawshab and Ibn Zayd hold that it speaks specifically to the rulers of the Muslims. Al-Tabari adopts this view and explains that the trusts are the public revenue and alms entrusted to the rulers, while he also reports Ibn Abbas taking it as an admonition by rulers to women who defy their husbands. Ibn Juraij links the revelation to the episode of the Kaaba key, which the Prophet took from Uthman ibn Talha and then returned, a story Ibn Kathir notes is widely known. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan and Qatada, followed by most scholars, argue that the wording is general and applies to every trust, to righteous and wicked alike, whatever the particular cause. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi add that judges must rule by evidence, with the burden on the claimant and the oath on the one who denies. All agree that the closing phrase, that God hears and sees, serves as both promise and warning.

This verse commands believers to obey God, obey His Messenger and obey those in authority among them, and to refer any dispute back to God and the Messenger. Al-Tabari, al-Samʻani and al-Zamakhshari take the holders of authority to be rulers and leaders, while Mujahid, Jabir ibn ʻAbd Allah, al-Hasan, ʻAta' and Abu al-ʻAliya understand them as scholars and jurists. ʻIkrima names Abu Bakr and ʻUmar, and Mujahid names the Companions of the Prophet. Al-Tabari concludes that rulers and leaders are the most accurate meaning, whereas Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Qayyim hold that the verse covers both groups. The commentators agree that obeying the Messenger means following his Sunna after his death, and that obedience to rulers applies only to what is right, based on the hadith that obedience is only due in what is good. As for referring disputes back, most say this means the Book and the Sunna, with Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi noting that during the Prophet's lifetime one would ask him directly. Those who reject analogy cite this passage, but al-Razi and al-Alusi see in it support for qiyas, since referring an unstated case to a stated one requires reasoning by comparison. Finally, the exegetes explain that the phrase better and fairer in outcome means that this referral is preferable in this life and better in its final consequence.

God expresses wonder at those who claim to believe in what was revealed to the Prophet and before him, yet want to take their disputes to the tagut, though they were commanded to reject it. The commentators agree the verse concerns hypocrites, and that claiming faith while seeking judgment from other than God and His Messenger contradicts that claim. The general meaning of tagut, whatever exceeds its limits and judges beyond revelation, is widely accepted. Its precise identity is disputed. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Muqatil take it to be Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, al-Suddi names Abu Burda al-Aslami, a soothsayer, al-Sha'bi mentions a soothsayer of Juhayna, and al-Hasan refers to idols before which lots were cast. The occasion of revelation, reported at length by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others, involves a quarrel between a hypocrite and a Jew, and according to some accounts Umar killed the hypocrite, which is why he was called al-Faruq. Several commentators, including Ibn Ashur, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, add that the verse's wording extends to anyone who prefers other judgments to God's law. The following verses describe such hypocrites who turn away when called to God's judgment, then swear they only intended goodness and reconciliation. God tells the Prophet to turn away from them, admonish them, and address them with an eloquent word that reaches their souls. Scholars differ on the phrase about the calamity that will befall them, some reading it as public exposure and others as the death of their companion.

This verse describes a stance of the hypocrites: when they are called to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger, they turn away from him with great aversion. The commentators explain that they refuse to come to him so that he may judge between them, and that they also prevent others from doing so. They agree that the verse concerns the hypocrites and that the reproach targets their wish to seek judgment from someone other than the Prophet, or from an authority opposed to revelation. The identity of the 'taghut' is disputed: Ibn Abbas and others say it is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf; al-Sha'bi and Mujahid say a soothsayer of Juhayna; al-Suddi says Abu Burda the Aslami soothsayer; al-Hasan says an idol or the divining arrows placed before idols. Many take it to mean any authority that departs from divine law. Several causes of revelation are reported, among them a dispute between a hypocrite and a Jew that ended with Umar killing the hypocrite in some accounts, and a dispute over blood money between the tribes of Qurayza and Nadir in others. Ibn Kathir holds that the verse is more general than any single occasion. Al-Razi argues that the verse implies that whoever rejects an order of Allah or His Messenger leaves Islam, while others regard this as an inference rather than the plain sense. Ibn Ashur notes that 'za'ama' can denote a doubtful or false claim, and that the hypocrites were originally Jews. The following verses warn the hypocrites of the consequences of their aversion and instruct the Prophet to turn away from them while admonishing them with words that reach their souls.

This verse describes hypocrites who turned away from the Prophet's judgment and then, after a calamity struck them because of their deeds, came to him swearing by God that they intended only good and reconciliation between the parties. The commentators gave the "calamity" two main readings: al-Zajjaj linked it to Umar's killing of a hypocrite who had rejected the Prophet's ruling, after which the man's tribe came demanding blood-money; others, including Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, took it as any punishment striking the hypocrites in this world and the next. al-Razi and al-Jubba'i understood it as humiliation and banishment from the Prophet's presence. As for "what their hands have sent forward," some took it to mean seeking judgment from someone other than the Prophet, others their earlier sins. Most explain "only good and conciliation" as reconciling the disputants and bringing the ruling closer to them, while Ibn Kaysan reads it as justice and truth. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di hold that real goodness lies in submitting to God and His Messenger, and that the oath is false. The verses that follow command the Prophet to turn away from them while admonishing them and speaking to them a far-reaching word. al-Hasan took this as a threat of death if they persisted in hypocrisy, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi took it as a threat of annihilation. al-Razi clarifies that turning away does not mean cutting off, but refraining from punishing them and accepting their excuses. Most commentators draw from the passage that the claim to faith is refuted by one who wants to be judged by something other than God's law.

This verse tells us that God knows what the hearts of these hypocrites hide, the ones who seek judgment from the tyrant and turn away from the Prophet ﷺ, and that their false oaths will not help them. The Prophet is told to turn away from punishing them or accepting their excuses, to admonish them with his tongue, and to speak to them about their own selves with an eloquent word that reaches their hearts. The commentators differ on what turning away means. Al-Tabari understands it as not punishing their bodies while warning them of God's punishment, while Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud take it as giving up punishment for a benefit in sparing them, or refusing their excuses. Al-Zamakhshari reads it as ignoring their turning away while continuing to counsel them. On the eloquent word, al-Hasan says it is a threat of death if they persist in hypocrisy, al-Tabari says it is commanding them to fear God and to believe in the Messenger and his promises and threats, and al-Razi says it is warning them of punishment in this world and the next. Al-Nasafi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that some consider the turning away abrogated by the verse of fighting, whereas Ibn 'Uthaymin rejects abrogation and holds that the verses on fighting and this one concern different matters. Several accounts of the occasion of revelation exist; the best known concerns a dispute between a hypocrite and a Jew brought to the Prophet and then to 'Umar, while others mention a quarrel between al-Zubayr and an Ansari over an irrigation channel. The commentators agree that the verse requires admonishing the hypocrites, and that words spoken privately reach the heart more effectively than public rebuke.

This verse states that God sent no messenger except to be obeyed, by His permission. It then says that if the hypocrites, who wronged themselves by seeking judgment from the false idol, had come to the Prophet in repentance, asked God's forgiveness, and had the Messenger ask forgiveness for them, they would have found God accepting of repentance and merciful. Most commentators agree on the general sense: the Prophet must be obeyed, and the door of repentance stays open to those who return. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Ibn Sa'di understand the 'permission of God' as His command or His help, and hold that the request for forgiveness must come with sincere regret and a sincere apology. Al-Zamakhshari and those who follow him explain that the shift from addressing the Prophet to speaking of him in the third person, in 'and the Messenger asked forgiveness for them', is meant to honour him. Opinions differ on the occasion of revelation: Mujahid and al-Sha'bi link it to a Jew and a hypocrite who went before Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf or 'Umar, while Ibn 'Abbas, 'Urwa and Umm Salama relate it to the dispute between al-Zubayr and an Ansari over irrigation water. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan take the verse as affirming that God accepts repentance. The well-known story of a Bedouin at the grave has been reported by some, but Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin consider it weak, so it is not relied upon here.

God swears by His own Lord that people do not truly believe until they make the Prophet ﷺ the judge in their disputes, then find no constriction or doubt in their hearts about his ruling, and submit to it fully, outwardly and inwardly. Commentators explain that "shajara baynahum" means that matters became entangled and disputed, and that "haraj" means constriction, doubt or sin: Mujahid takes it as doubt, al-Dahhak as sin, and others as tightness of the heart. On the occasion of revelation, opinions differ. Many, including the hadith of al-Bukhari transmitted by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, link it to the dispute between al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam and an Ansari over irrigating land from the stream of al-Harra: the Prophet ﷺ first told al-Zubayr to water his land and then release the water to his neighbour, and after the Ansari's anger he gave al-Zubayr his full right. Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and Ata', however, say it concerns a hypocrite and a Jew who wanted their case judged outside the Prophet's court. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer this second view because it follows the preceding verses, while Ibn al-Arabi and al-Qurtubi hold that the ruling is general and includes al-Zubayr's case. All agree that inner acceptance of the judgment is required, not merely outward compliance.

This verse says that had God ordered the hypocrites, as He had ordered the Children of Israel, to kill themselves or leave their homes, only a few would have done it. The commentators agree that the verse is a rebuke, and that obeying God and the Messenger is better for them and strengthens their faith when it is sincere. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the command in question is killing and exile, and that the verse shows how weak the resolve of many people is. They differ on who is meant by the pronoun in 'had We prescribed for them': Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean the hypocrites, while al-Razi holds that the opening is general and only the ending concerns the hypocrites. On recitation, most read 'qalilun' in the nominative as a substitute for the pronoun in 'fa'aluhu', while Ibn 'Amir reads it in the accusative as an exception. Several exegetes report that Thabit ibn Qays, Umar, Ammar and Ibn Mas'ud said that they would obey if commanded, and the Prophet then said that some of his community have faith firmer than mountains; al-Qurtubi and al-Razi note that some reports attribute the words to Abu Bakr. The commentators agree that the great reward and the guidance to the straight path are the fruit of obedience, and the next verse links that obedience to companionship with the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, a bounty from God according to Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari.

The commentators explain that this verse says that if God had required the hypocrites, as He had required the Children of Israel, to kill themselves or leave their homes, only a few would have done it. It then says that if they had followed what they were advised, it would have been better for them and would have strengthened their faith, and God would have given them a great reward from Himself and guided them to the straight path. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir understand the great reward as Paradise according to some, and the straight path as faith or the true religion, although al-Razi also suggests it may mean the path from the Final Gathering to Paradise. The commentators differ on the pronoun: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid refer it to the hypocrites, while al-Razi takes the address as general at the start and specific to the hypocrites at the end. Ibn 'Amir reads «qalilan» in the accusative, while the majority read «qalilun» in the nominative. Several occasions of revelation are reported, including Thabit ibn Qays saying that if commanded they would obey, and the Prophet replying that some in his community have faith firmer than mountains; others name Abu Bakr, Umar, Ibn Mas'ud and Ammar among the few. Ibn 'Ashur understands leaving one's homes as emigration and sees the verse as preparing for the call to jihad. Several commentators note that obedience is the cause of steadfastness in faith.

The commentators explain that the verse means that if God had imposed on people burdens that are hard on the soul, such as killing themselves or leaving their homes, only a few would have carried them out. Had they obeyed what they were admonished to do, it would have been better for them and would have made their faith firmer; God would have given them a great reward and guided them to the straight path. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the straight path to be the upright religion of God, that is Islam, while al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani mention the Quran or Islam, and Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi understand it as the true religion that keeps its followers steadfast. Al-Razi suggests it may mean the way to Paradise from the place of Resurrection, since it is mentioned after the reward. Al-Wahidi understands it as the religion of hanifiyya rather than Judaism. Al-Wahidi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan also report accounts of the occasion of revelation involving Thabit ibn Qays, Umar and Ibn Mas'ud, though these accounts do not settle the meaning. Ibn Juzayy, Ibn Ashur and Ibn Uthaymin hold that guidance includes both instruction and success, and that obedience is its path. Several scholars stress that this guidance is a grace of God rather than merely earned. In sum, the commentators agree that guidance to the straight path is the reward of obedience and steadfastness, while differing on the precise nature of that path.

This verse from Surat al-Nisa says that whoever obeys God and the Messenger will be with four groups whom God has favoured: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, and that these make excellent companions. The commentators agree that this companionship refers to the abode and its delights, not to an equal rank, since degrees differ; each person is content with his station and can see and visit the others, as al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur explain. On the meaning of the siddiqin, the truthful, opinions differ: al-Tabari takes it as an intensive form of truthfulness, meaning one whose deeds confirm his words, and cites a hadith in his commentary without ruling on its soundness, while others connect it with giving in charity. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi describe the siddiq as one who is abundantly truthful, and al-Razi holds that Abu Bakr deserves the title most, for being the first to believe the Prophet. The shuhada, the martyrs, are for most commentators those slain in God's cause, while others understand them as scholars who bear witness to the truth; Ibn Uthaymin combines both readings. The salihun, the righteous, are those whose inner and outer conduct is sound. Regarding the occasion of revelation, several reports are given, including that of a companion distressed at the thought of not seeing the Prophet in Paradise, and that of Thawban, his freedman; al-Tabari and others note that the wording is general. Grammarians discuss whether rafiq is a tamyiz or a hal, and why it appears in the singular. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that the prophets are mentioned before the truthful because the latter follow them.

This verse teaches that the companionship with the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous in Paradise is not a reward owed simply to good deeds, but a grace from God, and that God's knowledge of His servants and of what they deserve is complete. The commentators link it to obedience to God and His Messenger. Al-Tabari explains that the truthful (siddiqin) are those who confirm their words by their deeds, while others take them to be the followers of the prophets who were first to believe them, and Ibn Qutayba sees the word as meaning one who is very truthful. Most commentators say that martyrs are those killed in God's cause, whereas al-Razi holds that a martyr is one who bears witness to God's religion by argument and by the sword. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy report the occasions of revelation: companions anxious that they would not see the Prophet in Paradise, and the story of Thawban, his freedman. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Razi use the verse against the Mu'tazili view that God owes reward, while others simply read it as God's grace. On grammar, al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya record the debate between the Basran and Kufan grammarians over the word rafiq, whether it is a specification or a circumstantial accusative. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that the truthful follow the prophets, which is why the prophets are mentioned first, followed by the martyrs and then the righteous, each in their rank.

This verse commands the believers to take precautions against their enemy, meaning to be alert, prepared and armed, and then to go out to fight, either in successive groups or all together. The commentators agree that "thubat" is the plural of "thubba", a band or company, and that it means sending detachments one after another, or a single massed army with the Prophet ﷺ, as reported from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and others note that "hidhr" may mean the precaution itself or the weapon that protects, a reading favoured by al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean equipment and arms. Al-Alusi adds that precaution covers every kind of preparation.

Scholars differ on the verse's scope. Ibn Abbas and others regard it as abrogated by the verse saying the believers should not all go out together, whereas al-Qurtubi holds both verses valid, one for when a general mobilisation is needed and the other when a group suffices, jihad being a collective obligation. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir add that precaution does not turn away fate, but gives peace of mind. Most commentators link the verse to the hypocrites who lag behind: one of them says, if a misfortune strikes the believers, that God has blessed him for not being present, and if victory and spoils come, he wishes he had been there. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari suggest that the laggard may also discourage others, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi see the address as covering both sincere believers and hypocrites. Al-Kalbi and others take it to refer only to the hypocrites. Ibn Kathir stresses that martyrdom is a great favour and that the fighter is rewarded whether he is killed or victorious.

This verse describes a type of hypocrite who dragged his feet in fighting and discouraged others from joining. The commentators agree that the address is to the believers, meaning those who professed Islam and were counted among them. If a defeat or a loss struck the Muslims, this man rejoices that he was absent; if they won a victory and booty, he wishes he had been with them to share in it. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari report that the verse concerns the hypocrites, and Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari explain that the verb can mean that he himself holds back and also holds others back. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi hold that both meanings are intended together. Ibn al-Jawzi reports another view, that the verse refers to weak believers who lacked knowledge of religious rulings; al-Razi and al-Qurtubi reject this, finding it incompatible with what follows. Al-Zamakhshari reads the phrase "as if there had never been affection between you" as mockery. Readers differ between the intensive and the lighter form of the verb, and the grammarians note that the verbs batu'a, abta'a and battaa are close in meaning. All the commentators take "witness" to mean one present in the battle.

This verse describes people who hang back from fighting in God's cause and also discourage others. If a misfortune befalls the believers, such as a defeat or the death of fighters, they rejoice at having stayed behind and consider it a blessing from God. If instead the Muslims win a victory and booty, they wish they had been present to share in it. The commentators largely agree that this attitude comes from seeking worldly gain rather than the reward of jihad. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report, following Qatada and Ibn Jurayj, that the wish stems from envy, and that such people hope for no reward and fear no punishment for staying back. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and most exegetes take the words 'among you' to address the believers, with the laggards being hypocrites, since God distinguishes them from the believers. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi allow that the laggards may be weak believers who lacked religious knowledge. Scholars differ on where the clause 'as if there had never been affection between you and him' belongs. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi treat it as a parenthesis between the verb and its object, an ironic remark about the hypocrites. Al-Zajjaj, al-Maturidi and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi connect it to what precedes, while Ibn 'Ashur reads it as describing someone with no earlier bond to the believers. On the reading 'fa-afuza', the majority take the accusative as the answer to the wish, whereas al-Hasan and Yazid al-Nahwi read the nominative.

This verse exhorts the believers to fight in the cause of God, which the commentators explain as fighting to exalt His religion and spread His message. Those who « sell the life of this world for the Hereafter » are, in the commentators' reading, those who prefer the reward of the next life to the pleasures of this one. The commentators agree that whoever fights in God's path will either be killed as a martyr or win and prevail, and that a great reward awaits him in both cases, which many take to be Paradise. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state that the fighter receives this reward whether he is slain or victorious, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Abu Hurayra in which God guarantees that whoever sets out to fight in His cause will be admitted to Paradise or returned to his home with what he has gained of reward or booty. Al-Razi holds that the fighter must resolve himself to one of the two outcomes, death or victory.

The commentators differ on who is meant by « those who sell ». Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi take it to refer to sincere believers who prefer the Hereafter, while al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur allow that it may refer to the hypocrites who held back at Uhud, who buy the present life at the price of the Hereafter; al-Razi then supposes an ellipsis meaning « that they believe and then fight ». Al-Sa'di favours the view that the address is to the most steadfast believers, since they alone have prepared themselves for jihad.

As for the verb « yashrun », most read it as « to sell », while some also read it as « to buy ». Al-Zamakhshari cites a verse of Ibn Mufarrigh, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy record the view that it means « to sell ».

This verse urges the believers to fight in the cause of God and rebukes them for holding back. It recalls the weak men, women and children who were oppressed in Mecca and pressured to abandon their faith. They pray that God bring them out of this city whose people are wrongdoers, and that He appoint for them a protector (wali) and a helper (nasir). The commentators unanimously identify the city as Mecca. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the cause of God here as fighting to raise God's word, with the rescue of the oppressed included in it. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi offer two readings of the phrase "and the oppressed": either it is coordinated with "the cause of God", meaning in the cause of the oppressed, or it is in the accusative of specification.

The commentators agree that the oppressed were Muslims left in Mecca who were unable to emigrate, and that Ibn 'Abbas was among them together with his mother. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that mentioning the children shows the extremity of the polytheists' cruelty, and that their supplication is closer to being answered. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan add that "the children" may refer to slaves. According to most, the prayer was answered at the conquest of Mecca, when the Prophet appointed 'Attab ibn Usayd, who gave justice to the oppressed, as al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report.

On the grammar of the masculine qualifier "wrongdoing", al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi explain that it describes the people, the adjective attached to the city through a pronoun. Ibn 'Uthaymin draws from the verse that asking God to leave a city is permitted when one fears for one's faith. Ibn Sa'di and al-Qasimi see in it the obligation to fight to deliver oppressed Muslims.

This verse distinguishes the believers, who fight in the way of God, meaning in obedience to Him and to raise His religion, from the disbelievers, who fight in the way of the Taghut. Most commentators identify the Taghut with Satan, while some take it to mean anything worshipped besides God. God then commands the believers to fight the allies of Satan and assures them that Satan's scheme is weak. Al-Tabari explains that the unbelievers fight out of pride or envy, without hope of reward, whereas the believer fights with insight into what awaits him, whether he is killed or victorious. Al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di also take the Taghut to be Satan. Al-Wahidi and al-Sam'ani report that his scheme proved weak at Badr, when he fled upon seeing the angels. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read the verse as an encouragement meant to strengthen the believers' hearts. Al-Razi holds that intention, not the outward form of fighting, is what matters, and that God's support is stronger than Satan's. The verse is linked in most tafsirs to the context of the oppressed Muslims of Mecca who asked God to deliver them, a point that most commentators repeat, while Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri draw lessons on faith and on aiding the weak.

The commentators explain that this verse addresses a group of companions who, while still in Mecca, asked permission to fight the polytheists, and were told to hold back their hands and to keep up prayer and zakat. When fighting was prescribed for them in Medina, a group feared people with a fear equal to, or greater than, their fear of God, and said: "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? Would that You had delayed us to a near term." God tells His Prophet to reply that the enjoyment of this world is small, that the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of God, and that they will not be wronged by a hair's breadth. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari relate this occasion of revelation, and most see the fear as a natural human weakness rather than a rejection of God's command, as al-Hasan al-Basri holds. Mujahid, however, relates the verses to the Jews, while al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur favour the hypocrites, since the following passage concerns those who attribute evil to the Prophet. On the fortified towers, Qatada and Ibn Jurayj take them as fortified palaces, al-Sudi as palaces in the sky, and others as plastered structures. The grammarians also discuss the two readings of the word mushayyada. The fatil is the thread in the cleft of a date stone, a proverb for the smallest amount. Some readers read "they will not be wronged" with ya, others with ta.

This verse teaches that death will reach a person wherever he is, even within strong fortresses, and that caution does not avert what God has decreed. The commentators report that some people, whether hypocrites or Jews according to the reports, credited God for any good that came to them, but blamed the Prophet ﷺ for any harm, such as drought or defeat, as a bad omen. God replies that all of it comes from Him by His will and decree. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the good and the harm here mean prosperity and hardship, victory and defeat, not obedience and sin, although Ibn 'Ashur and al-Baydawi note that the words may also include obedience and wrongdoing. On the phrase "what befalls you of harm is from yourself", Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd take it to mean because of your sins, while al-Zamakhshari and others stress that the human being is the cause through his own deeds. On the "fortresses", Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj say palaces, al-Suddi and al-Rabi' say the constellations, and most say strongholds. Al-Razi and others discuss what the verse implies about divine decree and human action, which Ibn 'Ashur observes has been cited by both sides. Finally, most commentators read the closing remark as meaning that these people do not understand the Qur'an or grasp that everything comes from God.

The commentators explain that the good that reaches a person, such as prosperity or well-being, comes first from God's grace, while the harm that befalls him, such as hardship or misfortune, is due to his own sins, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report. Although the address is made to the Prophet ﷺ, its meaning extends to all people. Most exegetes take good and evil to mean concrete goods and calamities, such as fertility or drought, victory or defeat, health or sickness, which fall under God's decree. The action is ascribed to God as a bounty and to the human as a cause. Al-Tabari notes that some grammarians explained the particle (min) as reinforcing negation or as resembling a conditional, while others saw it as a matter of emphasis. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan mention various readings and interpretations, including one that treats the phrase as an implied question. Al-Mawardi, al-Razi and others link the verse to the refutation of the hypocrites and the Jews who blamed the Prophet ﷺ for misfortune. Al-Razi and al-Sa'di answer the apparent objection by distinguishing creation and decree from causation. The Mu'tazilites used the verse to argue that evil comes from human action, while the Sunni scholars read it as affirming that all things come from God; these readings are presented without the commentators deciding between them. The view that good means obedience and evil means disobedience, attributed to Abu al-Aliya, is considered weakly supported by Ibn al-Qayyim. Finally, the exegetes stress that the verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ, reminds him that his task is to convey the message, affirms God's witness to his prophethood, and states that he was sent to all people.

The plain meaning of the verse is that whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah, because the Messenger only commands and forbids what Allah has commanded and forbidden. As for whoever turns away, the Prophet is not responsible for watching over his deeds; his duty is only to convey the message. The commentators agree that the verse establishes the duty to obey the Prophet ﷺ as obedience to Allah, and that disobeying him is disobeying Allah. Al-Shafi'i draws from it that what Allah imposed without detailing it in the Quran can only be carried out through the Prophet's explanation, so his obedience is the very obedience of Allah. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim see in it evidence for the authority of the Sunna, whose additional rulings must be accepted. There is disagreement on the word hafiz: Ibn 'Abbas takes it to mean a watchman, al-Suddi and Ibn Qutayba a reckoner of deeds, and al-Zamakhshari a guarantor who punishes, while al-Razi considers turning away either inwardly or outwardly. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, report that the verse was revealed before the command to fight and was abrogated by the verse of the sword; Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur instead regard it as an established rule without abrogation, a matter of gentleness and preparation. Several reports give a cause of revelation, namely that hypocrites said the Prophet wanted to be taken as a lord as the Christians took Jesus, but Ibn Hajar did not find this narration. The following verses address hypocrites who say "obedience" and then plot otherwise at night: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain tabyit as deciding something by night, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that here the verb means secretly contriving.

This verse describes a group of hypocrites who, in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, said, "Obedience," but who, once they had left him, secretly planned something other than what they had professed. The apparent meaning, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, is that they altered or concealed what the Prophet had commanded. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it rather as falsifying and distorting his words. Al-Tabari, who develops the linguistic sense of the verb "bayyata," understands it as any matter decided at night or in secret, supporting this with lines of poetry; al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi follow this reading. Most commentators take the pronoun in "what you say" to refer to the Prophet, while Ibn Kathir refers it to the group itself. On "Allah records what they plot," al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the recording by the angels, whereas al-Zajjaj understands it as a revelation sent to the Prophet; al-Razi reports both views. As for "turn away from them," most read it as pardon and forbearance, al-Dahhak takes it as not disclosing their names, and several, including al-Wahidi, al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi and al-Suyuti, note that it was abrogated by the command to fight. Al-Razi disputes this, arguing that an absolute command to pardon cannot be abrogated by a later command. Several also observe that the nominative form of "obedience" signifies the stability of that obedience, and that Abu 'Amr and Hamza read with assimilation of the taa. The verse concludes that God suffices as a guardian against their schemes.

The plain meaning of the verse is that God rebukes the hypocrites for not reflecting on the Qur'an, and states that if it came from other than God they would find in it much contradiction. The commentators agree that the Qur'an is free from contradiction and inconsistency, but they differ on what kind of divergence is denied. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and most scholars take it to mean contradiction, while Muqatil and al-Zajjaj understand falsehood and error in reports of the unseen, al-Zajjaj adding disagreement about what the hypocrites conceal. Some Basran grammarians and al-Jubba'i read it as a gap between eloquence and what is base. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi stress that the Qur'an confirms its parts by one another, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb forbidding setting parts of the Qur'an against each other. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari see this consistency as proof of prophethood and as a call to reflection and against blind imitation. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the verse also invites reflection on the Qur'an's details. Al-Razi holds that apparent contradictions, such as those about seeing God or questioning on the Day of Judgment, are not real contradictions. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir hold that any apparent conflict should be attributed to the reader's limited understanding and referred to the learned. Most exclude variant readings and abrogation from the divergence meant, and keep only contradiction of meaning or unevenness of eloquence.

This verse teaches restraint in spreading news, especially reports about the expeditions of the Muslims, their security or their danger. According to the commentators, certain people, most of them identified as hypocrites, would immediately spread such reports without verifying them, and this harmed the believers. The verse asks that the news be referred to the Prophet ﷺ and to those in authority among the people of knowledge and judgment, so that those who can draw out its meaning decide what should be made public. The exegetes agree that the second part is addressed to the believers and that God's grace and mercy are what protect them from Satan. They differ, however, on what the exception 'except a few' refers to. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd, al-Farra' and al-Tabari attach it to the spreading of news: only a few did not spread it. Al-Hasan and Qatada attach it to those who seek to understand it; al-Dahhak attaches it to the following of Satan. Al-Razi and others also report that the few are those who were guided by their reason before the prophethood, such as Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl and Waraqa ibn Nawfal. Ibn Kathir cites the report of 'Umar about the rumour that the Prophet had divorced his wives, and some see the verse as a general rule against hasty publication of whatever one hears. Commentators draw from it support for consulting scholars and for the value of reasoned inference, while disapproving of repeating everything one hears without checking it.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to fight in His cause even alone, since he is charged only with his own action, and to urge the believers to fight. He promises that God may restrain the might of those who disbelieved, and that God is mightier in might and more severe in punishment. The commentators agree that the address is first to the Prophet, and that the opening particle links the command to the preceding call to jihad and the rebuke of those who held back. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report the occasion as the appointed meeting at Badr al-Sughra arranged with Abu Sufyan after Uhud: some disliked going out, the Prophet set out with seventy riders, and God averted the threat since Abu Sufyan did not come. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that the meaning is general, so no one should abandon jihad because others hold back. On 'asa from God, Ikrima, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take it as a binding promise, while al-Razi reads it as an encouragement to hope. They point to the restraint shown at Badr al-Sughra and Hudaybiyya. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi extend it to the scattering of the confederates and the expulsion of the Jews. Qatada and al-Hasan define tankil as an exemplary punishment that deters others.

This verse states that whoever intercedes for another in a good cause receives a share of its reward, while whoever intercedes in an evil cause bears a share of its burden, and God is capable of all things and watches over them. The commentators agree that intercession here means taking up another's cause, that a good one is lawful and done for God's sake, and that an evil one is the opposite. They differ on its scope. Al-Tabari holds that it concerns urging the believers to fight or discouraging them from it, while Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and al-Kalbi take it as general, covering every intercession between people. Ibn Abbas and Muqatil describe the good intercession as reconciling people and the bad one as spreading slander. Al-Sa'di broadens it to any help given to a good or bad act. The word kifl is also debated: al-Hasan and Qatada read it as the burden of sin, whereas al-Sudi, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd read it as a portion, citing the verse 57:28. For muqit the views vary: powerful, according to Ibn Abbas, al-Sudi, Ibn Zayd and al-Zubayr ibn Abd al-Muttalib; watchful, witnessing or provider of sustenance for others, linked to the word qut, food. Al-Tabari prefers the sense of power, while Abu Ubayda links it to sustenance. Several commentators cite the hadith urging intercession, and al-Hasan adds that the intercessor is rewarded even if his plea is not granted.

The commentators explain that this verse tells the one who is greeted to answer with a better greeting or at least one like it. The word tahiyya originally means a prayer for long life and well-being, and in the religious law it came to mean the greeting of peace. They agree that returning the greeting is obligatory, while initiating it is a strongly recommended sunna. Al-Hasan, Ata and most scholars hold that the better answer is to add mercy and then blessing: to

This verse declares that Allah is the only true deity and that He will gather all people on the Day of Resurrection, a day about which there is no doubt. The commentators agree that this gathering means resurrection and assembly for reckoning and recompense. The implied oath, marked by the lam and the emphatic nun in "layajma'annakum", underlines the seriousness of the announcement against those who deny it. Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud take the question "wa man asdaqu mina Allahi hadithan" as a negation, meaning that no one is more truthful than Allah in His report, promise or threat. Al-Zamakhshari argues that lying is impossible for God, since lying arises from need, ignorance or foolishness, none of which apply to Him. Al-Razi links the two halves of the verse: mention of divine oneness points to monotheism, and the mention of the gathering points to justice, as God will judge between the wronged and the wrongdoers. On why the Day is called al-Qiyama, opinions differ: some say it is because people rise from their graves, others because they stand for judgment, and no one of these views is preferred over the others. Regarding the particle "ila", al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari take it as referring to death or the grave, while Abu Hayyan notes it can mean "in". Most commentators connect this verse to what precedes it, reinforcing the warning about the reckoning.

This verse addresses the believers, rebuking them for splitting into two camps over the hypocrites, since God has returned them to the state of disbelievers because of what they earned. The commentators explain that arkasa means to send back or overturn; Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, takes it to mean returning them, Qatada to mean destroying them, and as-Suddi to mean leading them astray. The verse concludes that whom God leads astray, no one can guide.

The commentators agree that the address is to the believers and that the hypocrites were people who outwardly professed Islam while concealing disbelief. They differ on the occasion of revelation. Al-Bukhari and Muslim, through Zayd ibn Thabit, relate that it concerned those who turned back at Uhud, whereas Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and others mention people who emigrated and then apostatized, or the affair of the slander. Al-Tabari prefers the Meccan account, because the following verse requires emigration, which would not apply to people of Medina. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi mention several of these views without settling them.

On the legal side, the verse that follows orders the believers not to take the hypocrites as allies until they emigrate, and to seize and kill them if they refuse. Exempted are those who join a people bound to the Muslims by a treaty, and those whose hearts recoil from fighting either side. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that some early scholars held this ruling to be abrogated by the verse of Bara'a, and Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn Abbas said the same. Al-Baghawi and al-Wahidi mention the same exemptions. The commentators also note that the grammar of fi'atayn is disputed, with the Basrans treating it as a circumstantial accusative and the Kufans as the predicate of an implied verb.

This verse reveals that the hypocrites wish the believers would disbelieve as they themselves have, so that everyone would be equal in unbelief. Therefore God forbids the believers to take these people as allies until they emigrate in the way of God, that is, until they leave the land of polytheism for the land of Islam and prove their faith through genuine emigration. If they turn away, the believers are to seize them and kill them wherever they find them, and not take them as friends or helpers. The commentators agree that the pronoun in 'they wish' refers to the hypocrites, and that the verse exposes the wickedness of their intention and warns the believers against them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the emigration meant is the move from the abode of disbelief to the abode of Islam, and that 'turning away' means refusing it according to Ibn 'Abbas, while al-Suddi takes it to mean openly showing their disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand emigration more broadly, as abandoning what God has forbidden, citing the hadith that the emigrant is one who forsakes what God has prohibited. The reports of the occasion of revelation differ: some concern those who withdrew from the battle of Uhud, others people who stayed in Mecca or went to join the polytheists. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was abrogated by the verse of Repentance, and Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi note the debate over whether emigration remained obligatory after the conquest of Mecca. As for the next verse, which makes exceptions, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy report that it was abrogated, while Ibn Sa'di stresses that the mention of emigration applies to those living in the land of disbelief.

This verse clarifies that the hypocrites whom the believers were ordered to seize and kill if they turn away from emigration and sincere faith may be spared in two cases. The first is those who take refuge with a people bound to the Muslims by a covenant, who then share that people's status and whose blood is protected. The second is those who come to the Muslims with hearts constricted at the idea of fighting either the Muslims or their own people, and who fight neither. Commentators name various peoples: the Banu Mudlij, Khuza'a, the Banu Bakr ibn Zayd Manat, or the Aslam tribe. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi reject Abu Ubayda's reading that the verb yasilun means 'to be affiliated by kinship', since kinship does not prevent fighting, as the Prophet fought the Quraysh who were his own kin. They prefer the meaning of seeking refuge, protection and alliance. As for 'had God willed, He would have given them power over you', most explain it as God casting fear into their hearts, while al-Jubba'i, as reported by al-Razi, understood it as strengthening their resolve to defend themselves. On abrogation, the majority, including Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, hold that the verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword in Surat al-Tawba, whereas al-Asamm argued it is not abrogated if it refers to an ally. The word salam means peace or submission, and the verse forbids harming those who stay out of the fighting and lay down their arms.

This verse describes a group of hypocrites who profess Islam before the Prophet ﷺ and his companions in order to be safe, while aligning with their polytheist kin and worshipping their idols so that they will be spared by them as well. Whenever they are brought back to idolatry or to fighting the Muslims, they fall back into it headlong. It commands that if they do not keep away from the Muslims, do not offer peace, and do not restrain their hands, they should be seized and killed wherever they are found, since this provides clear proof against them. The commentators agree that these are hypocrites whose treachery is evident, and that the order to fight them is conditional on their not withdrawing and not submitting; the groups mentioned in the preceding verse are not included.

Scholars differ on who these people were. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and al-Kalbi identify them with the clans of Asad and Ghatafan, who declared Islam near Medina and then returned to their people to reject it. Mujahid says they were people of Mecca who professed Islam for show and then went back to the idols; Qatada says they were people of Tihama who asked the Prophet for safe conduct; and al-Suddi attributes the verse to Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i. Al-Hasan simply identifies them as hypocrites.

They also disagree on the verse's scope. Al-Hasan, Qatada, 'Ikrima and, according to one transmission, Ibn 'Abbas hold that it was abrogated by the verse of the sword in Surat al-Tawba. Al-Razi and the majority hold that the prohibition on killing those who withdraw and seek peace remains valid, and that the command to fight applies only to those who fight. As for fitna, most take it to mean disbelief, while some take it to mean trial, and the "clear authority" is explained either as a manifest proof or as a permission to kill.

This verse states that it is not fitting for a believer to kill another believer, except by mistake. Whoever kills a believer by mistake must free a believing slave and pay full blood money to the victim's heirs, unless they waive it as charity. Al-Tabari reports that the verse was revealed concerning 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, who killed al-Harith ibn Yazid thinking him still an unbeliever, and Ibn Kathir also mentions a report about Abu al-Darda'. The commentators agree that the liberation of a slave is owed by the killer from his own property, while the blood money is borne by the killer's paternal kin, the 'aqila, who may pay it in instalments over three years. If the victim is a believer from a people at war with the Muslims, only the liberation is required, with no blood money, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and others. If the victim belongs to a people bound by a treaty, blood money is due along with the liberation. The scholars differ on the value of the blood money for a non-Muslim: one third according to al-Shafi'i, one half according to Malik and Ahmad, and the full amount according to Abu Hanifa. The standard amount is one hundred camels, or a thousand dinars, or twelve thousand dirhams. Whoever cannot find a slave must fast two consecutive months as repentance. On intentional killing, the text is extremely severe. The commentators differ on whether repentance is accepted: Ibn 'Abbas denies it, whereas the majority accept it.

This verse states that whoever deliberately kills a believer will have Hell as his recompense, abiding in it, with God's wrath and curse upon him and a tremendous punishment prepared. The commentators agree that this is among the gravest sins, yet they differ on several points. Ibn 'Abbas, according to a transmission cited by Ibn Kathir, and with him Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Hurayra and Ibn 'Umar, held that the killer has no repentance. The majority of scholars, both early and later, maintain that sincere repentance is accepted between the killer and God, and Ibn Kathir adds that the victim's right remains, God compensating him on the Day of Judgment. Al-Tabari reads the phrase "his recompense is Hell" as "if He recompenses him," since God may forgive and not make the punishment eternal; al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Atiyya lean in a similar direction. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Qayyim explain that khulud denotes a very long stay rather than endless duration, while the Mu'tazila take it in its strict sense. Some exegetes restrict the verse to one who kills considering the act lawful, and others tie it to the episode of Miqyas ibn Subaba, as Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud report. On abrogation, Ibn 'Abbas held that the verse was never abrogated, while others place it six months after the sura al-Furqan, and many reject abrogation of a statement of fact. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the debate mainly concerns how this verse fits with the verses on forgiveness. Thus the commentators agree on the gravity of the crime but divide between literal, admonitory and repentance-oriented readings.

The commentators explain this verse, which orders believers who set out to fight in God's cause to verify and make certain before killing, and forbids them to say to one who greets them with peace that he is not a believer, seeking the goods of this world, since with God are abundant spoils. The verse recalls their own state before Islam, when they hid their faith out of fear for themselves, until God favoured them by honouring them with the religion. The scholars agree that verification before killing is obligatory, and that people are judged in this world by their outward appearance, while hearts belong to God. They differ on the reading: most read 'fatabayyanu', meaning to clarify, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'fatathabbatu', meaning to be steadfast; Ibn 'Atiyya considers the former stronger, while Abu 'Ubayd and others see the two as close in meaning. On the greeting, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read 'al-salam' as submission, while the rest read it as the greeting; al-Tabari prefers submission as covering all the meanings reported. As for the occasion of revelation, the reports name different people: Muhallim ibn Jaththama and 'Amir ibn al-Adbat in some accounts, Usama ibn Zayd and Mirdas ibn Nahik in others, and al-Miqdad or Abu al-Darda' in still others. Al-Qaffal holds that these reports do not conflict and that the verse may have come down on several occasions. Al-Tabari reads 'as you were before' as meaning that you concealed your faith among the polytheists, which he considers the most correct view, while others take it as a reminder that you were once disbelievers before being guided.

This verse states that believers who stay behind without a valid excuse are not equal to those who strive in God's cause with their wealth and their persons. God has favoured the strivers over the stay-behinds by one degree, then by further degrees, forgiveness and mercy. The commentators agree that the 'people of harm', meaning those with a genuine excuse such as blindness, lameness, sickness or infirmity, are excluded from this reproach if their intention is sincere. Al-Tabari reports through several chains that the exception was revealed after Ibn Umm Maktum, who was blind, asked whether he could be granted a dispensation, and he favours the reading with the accusative, making it an exception. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi set out the three readings of the word 'ghayr' and their grammatical consequences. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the excused man receives the same reward as the fighter, while al-Qurtubi judges the view that he receives an equal reward to be more sound, though the fighter is still preferred for his direct action. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan take the 'degree' to mean superiority of rank, and the 'degrees' to be the levels of Paradise. Ibn Muhayriz speaks of seventy years of travel between two of these degrees, and al-Razi and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith of the hundred degrees reserved for those who strive. Some scholars draw from the verse that jihad is a collective obligation rather than an individual one, since God also promises the good reward to those who stay behind. Most commentators understand 'al-husna' to mean Paradise.

This verse states that God raised those who strive, with their wealth and their persons, above those who stay back without excuse, while promising the good reward to all. The commentators agree on the reality of this superiority and on the special position of those prevented by a genuine impediment such as blindness, lameness or illness, who are not counted among the blameworthy who stay back. On the meaning of 'degrees', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take them to be the ranks of Paradise, while Qatada and Ibn Zayd see them as merits earned through Islam, emigration, struggle and martyrdom, and Ibn Zayd identifies them with the seven rewards listed in Surat al-Tawba. Ibn Muhayriz counts seventy degrees, between each two of which lies the distance a thoroughbred covers in seventy years, and a hadith from Abu Sa'id speaks of a hundred degrees in Paradise reserved for fighters. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya distinguish the single degree of merit from the plurality of degrees. Ibn Juzayy and others note the readings of the word 'ghayr' in the nominative, accusative and genitive, each with its grammatical meaning. Al-Razi holds that the disabled may equal the fighters if their intention is sincere, while al-Tabari and Ibn al-Qayyim distinguish those held back despite a firm intention. Jurists draw from the verse that jihad is a collective obligation, since God promises the good reward to those who stay back as well.

This verse describes those who had accepted Islam in Mecca but did not emigrate to Medina although they were able to. When the angels take their souls while they are wronging themselves by remaining in the land of polytheism, they ask: 'In what were you?' They reply that they were oppressed in the land, and the angels respond that God's earth was spacious and they should have emigrated. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that it was revealed concerning Meccans who professed Islam, then went out with the polytheists to Badr and were killed there; Ibn Abbas and Ikrima add that some of them apostatised under pressure. Al-Dahhak took them to be hypocrites who stayed behind with the Prophet. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi hold that emigration was then obligatory for anyone unable to practise his religion. The verse excepts the truly oppressed men, women and children who cannot find a way out and hopes for God's pardon for them; Ibn Abbas said he and his mother were among them. Several commentators note that the obligation of hijra ended with the conquest of Mecca, while others draw from the verse a general rule requiring a Muslim to leave any land where he cannot practise his religion. The following verse promises that whoever emigrates in God's cause and dies on the way has his reward secured with God, and that emigration gives the believer abundant refuge and provision on earth. Commentators agree that the verse urges emigration and warns against staying behind when one is able to leave, while those who are genuinely powerless are excused.

This verse describes the fate of those who die while wronging themselves by remaining behind when they were able to emigrate. The angels, as they take their souls, ask them what their condition was, and they answer that they were oppressed in the land; the angels reply that God's earth was wide and they should have migrated, so their abode is Hell. The commentators agree that the exception in the verse covers the truly weak men, women and children who have no means to leave and do not know the way. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others, the verse was revealed about some Meccans who had embraced Islam but did not emigrate, and some of whom were killed fighting with the polytheists at Badr; Ibn Abbas and his mother are cited as among the excused weak. Al-Tabari understands the wrongdoing as earning God's anger, whereas al-Razi and al-Baydawi take it to mean disbelief or disobedience. Ibn Atiyya holds that one who dies as an apostate is a disbeliever who remains in Hell forever, while one who dies sinful remains there without eternity. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir regard emigration as obligatory for every convert, while Ibn Sa'di calls it one of the greatest duties, abandoning it a major sin. The commentators explain 'hila' as the ability, means and provision for the journey, and 'sabil' as the road to Medina or any route to deliverance. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari explain that 'asa' from God conveys hope or, for others, certainty, so that the one who did not emigrate is given hope of pardon. The following verse promises that whoever emigrates in God's way will find refuge and abundance, and that the one who dies on the way has his reward secured with God.

This verse addresses those who embraced Islam in Mecca but stayed there and did not emigrate to Medina. When the angels take their souls while they are wronging themselves by remaining, they ask them what their state in their religion was. They answer that they were oppressed on earth, and the angels reply that Allah's earth was spacious and they should have emigrated. The commentators state that their final abode is Hell. The verse then excepts the truly oppressed men, women and children who cannot find a way out or a path, and hopes that Allah will pardon them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi agree that the verse was revealed about some Meccans who had accepted Islam and then went out with the polytheists to Badr and were killed there. Tawaffa means the taking of souls, and the angels may refer to the Angel of Death and his assistants. On the meaning of wronging oneself, Ibn Abbas and most commentators take it as disbelief, al-Suddi as failing to emigrate, and others as a grave sin; al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also mention hypocrisy. On the children, al-Zamakhshari speaks of adolescents, while al-Razi means young children. Most read 'asa' as an expression of hope, though al-Hasan takes it as binding, and Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi see it as stressing how serious abandoning emigration is. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that emigration is obligatory for one who is able to do it and lives where his faith is endangered, while Ibn Ashur holds that this ruling ended with the conquest of Mecca. Ibn Abbas counted himself and his mother among the weak. The following verse, on the reward of one who dies while emigrating, is discussed through the story of Jundab ibn Damra.

This verse states that whoever emigrates in the way of God, that is, leaves a land of idolatry to protect his religion and settle where he can practise it, will find on earth many a refuge and abundant room, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others explain. The commentators differ on the meaning of "muraghaman": Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' take it as moving from one land to another, Mujahid as withdrawing from what is disliked, al-Suddi as seeking a livelihood, and Ibn Zayd as the emigration itself. As for "sa'a", most understand it as material ease and provision, while Qatada takes it as moving from error to guidance and from poverty to wealth, and al-Tabari includes all senses of relief and deliverance. The scholars agree that whoever leaves as an emigrant and dies before reaching his destination has his reward confirmed with God by His grace. The verse is said to have been revealed about a sick man of Khuza'a or Layth who was carried toward Medina and died at al-Tan'im, though the reports differ on his name. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi note that the ruling is general, covering any emigration for a religious purpose such as seeking knowledge, pilgrimage or fighting. Some have drawn from it that a warrior who dies before battle keeps his share of the spoils, while others limit the verse to the reward alone. The commentators do not settle these views and present them as they stand.

This verse grants permission to shorten the prayer while travelling, with no blame attached. It names the fear of disbelievers' attack as a condition, but most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, explain that this condition reflects the typical dangers of journeys in the Prophet's time, and that shortening is permitted in safety too, as the Sunna shows, including through the report of Umar's question and the Prophet's reply that it is a charity from God. Al-Tabari distinguishes between shortening the number of units and shortening the manner of prayer in danger, and most of the verse's commentators link it to the prayer of fear described in the following verses. The jurists differ on whether shortening is obligatory: Abu Hanifa, Umar, Ali and Ibn Umar consider it obligatory, whereas al-Shafi'i sees it as a permission and Malik as a recommended practice. On the minimum distance, Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad cite four barids, Abu Hanifa three days' journey, and the Zahiris accept any journey. The forms of prayer in fear are reported in various ways, and all agree that the believers must keep their arms and remain alert.

This verse sets out how to pray the prayer of fear when the enemy is near. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, the Prophet ﷺ leads one group in prayer while the other faces the enemy; when the first group completes its prostration, it moves behind to guard, and the second group comes to pray with him. Commentators differ on who must take up arms: Ibn 'Abbas says it is the group facing the enemy, al-Shafi'i says those praying with the imam, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the command applies to both groups to make them more intimidating to the enemy. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi report that most scholars hold this procedure continues after the Prophet ﷺ, with the imams as his deputies, whereas Abu Yusuf and Ibn 'Ulayya restricted it to his presence. The reports of the prayer vary: Malik and al-Shafi'i follow the hadith of Sahl ibn Abi Hathma from Dhat al-Riqa', while Abu Hanifa follows that of Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi consider all the authentic forms valid. The verse also allows laying down weapons in case of rain that causes harm or illness, while remaining vigilant. Finally it notes that God has prepared a humiliating punishment for the disbelievers, and that taking precautions is an act of obedience and a use of means, not a sign of fear of their strength.

This verse teaches that after completing the prayer, especially the prayer of fear, the believer should remember God constantly, standing, sitting, or lying down. When the fear has passed and they feel secure, they should perform the prayer in its full form. The commentators agree that the prayer is an obligation fixed to specific times. They differ on the meaning of 'when you are secure'. Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it to mean returning home, when the traveller must pray the full number of units instead of shortening them, while al-Sudi, Ibn Zayd and al-Zajjaj understand it as the end of danger. Al-Tabari prefers the second view, since the verse distinguishes two situations, great fear and safety. On 'a decree with fixed times', Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Sudi explain it as an obligation prescribed, while Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada and Zayd ibn Aslam stress that the prayer has set times. Al-Tabari favours the latter while noting that the two meanings are close. Several exegetes, including al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, report the different forms of the prayer of fear transmitted in hadiths, and most scholars accept all the authentic forms. Abu Yusuf and al-Muzani, however, held that this prayer was specific to the Prophet, a view most commentators do not adopt.

In this verse God urges the believers not to weaken or slacken in pursuing their enemy in battle, and reminds them that the pain of wounds afflicts the enemy too, so suffering is not theirs alone. The commentators agree on the general sense of encouragement to jihad. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi, the verse was revealed after the Battle of Uhud, when the Prophet sent men after Abu Sufyan and his army as they withdrew, and the Muslims complained of their wounds.

The main difference concerns the word "hope" in "you hope from God what they do not hope". Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Nasafi, al-Sam'ani and Ibn al-Jawzi, take it to mean hope for reward and victory. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, as reported by al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, say it can mean fear, that is, you fear from God what they do not fear, though they hold that this usage occurs only with a negation. Al-Razi adds that believers worship a hearing and seeing God whose reward may be hoped for, while idolaters worship idols.

The readings also differ, especially on the verb for "you suffer" and on the particle "that you are". Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi see the verse as a rational argument showing that the pain is shared, while al-Baydawi and al-Shawkani read it as the reason for forbidding weakness. Ibn al-Qayyim draws a broader lesson about the trials of believers.

God addresses His Prophet, affirming that He sent down the Book with truth so that he might judge between people by what God has shown him, and that he should not become an advocate for the treacherous. The commentators agree that these verses concern the case of Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who stole a coat of mail from his neighbour Qatada ibn al-Nu'man and hid it with a Jew; his tribe asked the Prophet to clear him, and he was inclined to do so until the revelation exposed the truth. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the Prophet did not actually plead the case but only intended to, which is why he was told to seek forgiveness; Ibn 'Atiyya argues that such a plea implies no real sin, since the Prophet defended outward appearances while believing in their innocence. On the phrase 'what God has shown you', al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi allow either revealed knowledge or personal reasoning, al-Razi holds that judgement rested on revelation alone, many scholars cite it as evidence for the legitimacy of ijtihad, and al-Qurtubi quotes 'Umar warning against saying 'I judged by what God showed me'. All condemn defending a wrongdoer, recall that God does not love the treacherous sinner, and stress the gravity of falsely accusing an innocent person. They differ on who the traitor was, on who the innocent man was (the Jew Zayd ibn al-Samin, Labid ibn Sahl, or Abu Mulayl), and on whether the Prophet actually pleaded or merely considered it.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to seek God's forgiveness, after reminding him that the Book was sent down with truth so that he may judge between people by what God has shown him, and that he should not argue on behalf of the treacherous. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya, connect the verse to the case of Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who stole a coat of mail and planted it with an innocent Jew. The Prophet ﷺ was inclined to defend his own people until revelation cleared the Jew and exposed the thief. On the meaning of seeking forgiveness, opinions differ. Al-Tabari holds that it concerns the pleading on behalf of the traitors. Ibn 'Atiyya argues that the Prophet only defended outward appearances while believing them innocent, so it was no sin, and the verse addresses the sinners of his community. Al-Baghawi and Muqatil take it as repentance for wanting to punish the Jew or for the pleading. Abu al-Su'ud links it to having relied on their testimony. Al-Razi suggests it concerns having taken up their defence or intended to. Ibn 'Uthaymin concludes that the Prophet could commit a fault, and that judges must be patient. Al-Qurtubi reports the view that it may be a formula of glorification, not repentance for a specific sin.

This verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ, though the instruction is meant for the community: do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves through disobedience, since the harm of their betrayal falls back on them, and God does not love one who is a habitual traitor and sinner. The commentators agree that it was revealed about Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who stole a coat of mail and hid it with a Jew, while his clan pleaded for him before the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the Prophet ﷺ excused him, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya argues that this was no sin, since he judged by outward appearances while believing them innocent. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baghawi link the plea for forgiveness to the Prophet's intention to punish the Jew. Al-Razi observes that the intensive forms khawwan and athim point to a habit of repeated betrayal, and Ibn 'Ashur explains that betraying oneself means acting against one's own interest, with the prohibition aimed at the community more than at the Prophet. Al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi see the verse as a general warning against aiding wrongdoers, while Ibn al-'Uthaymin draws from it that betrayal is a major sin. The sources differ on the identity of the wrongly accused: some name the Jew Zayd ibn al-Samin, others name Labid ibn Sahl or Abu Mulayl.

This verse describes people who hide from others out of shame and fear of disgrace, yet do not hide from God, who is with them when they plot by night words He does not approve. Nearly all commentators connect the verse to the affair of Ṭu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who stole a coat of mail, hid it with an innocent man, and whose people then asked the Prophet ﷺ to defend him. Al-Ṭabarī explains that tabyīt means to prepare or devise at night, and he reports from Abū Razīn that it means to compose, a meaning he considers close to the first; he also mentions the view that it means to change. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī treat calling a mere intention a 'word' as a figure of speech, or as inner speech, while al-Nasafī takes it as evidence that speech is the meaning held in the soul. Ibn Kathīr and Ibn Juzayy say the passage was revealed about this affair and rebukes those who argued for the guilty. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn al-Jawzī add that it covers anyone who acts in the same way. On God's being with them, most read it as knowledge and awareness, al-Rāzī adding power and sight, while Ibn ʿUthaymīn sees both a warning and a real presence alongside God's exaltation above creation. Al-Ālūsī notes that hiding from God can only be understood figuratively, as shame. The disagreements concern mainly the sense of God's presence and the nature of speech, not the overall meaning of the verse.

This verse addresses those who argued on behalf of the Banu Ubayriq, and especially Ṭu'ma, to defend them against a theft accusation. It tells them that they may have defended these people in the life of this world, but no one can plead for them before God on the Day of Resurrection, nor stand as their guardian against His punishment. The commentators explain that human argument can prevail among people in this world, but nothing is hidden from God. All agree that the verse concerns the theft of a coat of mail, which Ṭu'ma tried to pin on an innocent Jew. Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr and al-Baghawī read the surrounding verses as one continuous passage on the hypocrites, whereas Ibn 'Aṭiyya and Ibn al-Jawzī take 'them' to mean only the thief. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari explain that jidāl means fierce contention, and that the question form carries rebuke. Ibn Kathīr and Ibn Juzayy report the occasion of revelation in detail, while Ibn 'Ashur stresses that the target is the tribal partisans who defended the guilty man. Ibn 'Uthaymin draws the lesson that it is forbidden to plead for someone known to be in the wrong. The commentators agree on the core meaning and differ mainly on who is addressed and on the narrative details.

This verse opens the door of repentance to anyone who commits an evil or wrongs himself and then seeks God's forgiveness, for he will find God Forgiving and Merciful. Several commentators link it to the story of Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who stole a coat of mail and blamed a innocent Jew, so God offered him and his clan the chance to repent. Al-Tabari, however, takes the meaning in general terms, applying to every sinner even though the revelation came in that context. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report sayings from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud encouraging repentance, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith in which the Prophet promises forgiveness to one who prays two units after ablution and then asks pardon. On what istighfar requires, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan hold that asking forgiveness without genuine repentance is not enough, while others, notably the Sunni scholars cited by Abu Hayyan, make it subject to God's will. The commentators differ on the difference between an "evil" and a "wrong to oneself". Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir understand the first as harm to others and the second as harm limited to the doer, such as a false oath. Ibn Atiyya, however, says the two phrases mean the same thing and are repeated for emphasis. Al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi say the "evil" is a sin short of polytheism, and the "wrong to oneself" is polytheism. Al-Alusi and al-Qasimi also follow these readings.
