This part of the verse states that whoever commits a sin bears its consequence and harm himself alone, and that it does not fall on others, while God is all-knowing of His servants' deeds and wise in recompensing them. Al-Tabari explains that this refers to one who commits a wrong deliberately and knowingly, and that he alone bears its burden and shame, adding that the verse forbids believers from defending the traitors, since defending them makes them like them. The commentators agree that the occasion of revelation was the affair of Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who stole a coat of mail and blamed a Jew, yet they agree that the wording is general and covers anyone who commits a sin. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan hold that khati'a and ithm may share the same meaning and that the repetition is for emphasis, whereas al-Tabari distinguishes them: a khati'a may be committed with or without intention, while ithm arises only from intention. Others, such as al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, contrast a minor fault with a major one. Ibn Kathir draws from the verse that no one bears another's burden, citing the verse saying that no bearer of burdens will bear the load of another. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi explain that kasb means what a person gains for his own benefit or to ward off harm, which is why it is not used for God's acts. Ibn 'Ashur notes that ithm here refers to a grave sin. All of them agree on the principle of personal responsibility, while differing on the finer linguistic points.

This verse states that whoever commits a wrong or a sin and then pins it on an innocent person has taken on a slander and a manifest sin. The commentators, following al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, agree that the verse was revealed about the affair of Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who stole a coat of mail and hid it with an innocent man. They differ on who that man was. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Ibn Sirin and Qatada say he was a Jew named Zayd ibn al-Samin, while Qatada ibn al-Nu'man, al-Suddi and Muqatil say he was a Muslim, either Labid ibn Sahl or Abu Mulayl al-Ansari. Al-Dahhak reports from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse concerns 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his accusation against 'A'isha. On the difference between khati'a and ithm, al-Tabari holds that a wrong may be committed unintentionally while sin requires deliberate intent; others see the minor and major sin, or two synonyms repeated for emphasis. Al-Razi distinguishes a fault that affects only its doer from a sin that harms others. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the accuser is both guilty of the sin and a liar by pinning it on another. Commentators also debate what the pronoun in 'bihi' refers to: the sin, the earning, or either one. Although the occasion is specific, most scholars take the wording as general, covering anyone who does the same.

This part of verse 4:113 describes God's favour upon His Prophet ﷺ: by His grace and mercy He protected him from a group, among the relatives of Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who plotted to lead him astray so that he would defend their companion, the thief, and clear him. The commentators agree that this scheme did not succeed and that its harm falls only on those who devised it, not on the Prophet. God also sent down the Book and wisdom to him and taught him what he did not know, which is presented as the greatest part of His favour. Most exegetes link the verse to the theft attributed to an innocent Jew, but many note that its wording is general. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari identify the group as the Banu Zafar, while Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by Ibn al-Jawzi, also mentions a delegation from Thaqif. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the pronoun may refer to people in general. On wisdom, Ibn 'Abbas understood it as inspired judgment, al-Shafi'i and others as the Sunnah, while Ibn al-Qayyim gave the sense of knowing the truth and acting upon it. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that prophethood is the greatest of favours. Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that divine protection reminds the believer to keep asking for steadfastness.

This verse states that most secret conversations between people contain no good, except those that call to charity, to a good deed, or to reconciliation between people; whoever does this seeking Allah's pleasure will be given a great reward. The commentators agree on the general sense: a rebuke of idle private talk and a praise of talk that concerns good works. Al-Tabari takes the word najwa to mean the group of those conversing, so the exception is a direct one; he explains that ma'ruf is whatever Allah has commanded or recommended of righteous deeds, and that reconciliation means bringing together those in dispute within what Allah has permitted. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi hold that the exception may be disconnected, meaning that whoever commands charity has good in his conversation, while al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi regard both readings as possible. Concerning ma'ruf, Ibn Abbas and Muqatil took it to mean the obligatory duty, while others understand it as lending, aiding someone in distress, or any act of kindness, the view most commentators favour. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di stress that reconciliation is general, covering lives, property and honour, and that sincere intention is required to earn the reward. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Uthaymin note that a deed done for show earns no reward. Ibn Kathir reports that al-Shafi'i used the verse as evidence that consensus is binding, whereas al-Shawkani disputes that conclusion. Abu Hayyan notes that although the verse was revealed concerning Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, its meaning is general.

This verse states that whoever deliberately opposes the Messenger ﷺ after guidance has become clear to him, and follows a path other than that of the believers, will be left to what he has chosen and cast into Hell, a dreadful destination. The commentators agree that the occasion of revelation is Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who apostatised and fled to Mecca after his theft was exposed, and some report that he died in polytheism. Al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari hold that the verse applies to any opposition to the Prophet in belief, worship or law. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi extend the threat to those who depart from the way of the believers, meaning the consensus of the community, and draw from it the prohibition of opposing consensus. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi use the verse as evidence that consensus is binding, an argument al-Shafi'i is said to have reached after reading the Quran three hundred times. Al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur find this inference inconclusive, since "the way of the believers" may mean faith itself or submission to the Prophet, and Ibn 'Uthaymin repeats the reasoning while warning that many claimed consensuses are not sound. Al-Tabari explains that "what he chose" refers to idols that neither benefit nor protect. Al-Zamakhshari reads "We will leave him to what he chose" as God forsaking him, while Ibn Sa'di reads it as God making his choice appealing to him as a gradual test that deepens his error. Al-Razi also notes that responsibility presupposes knowledge of the right way, which Ibn 'Uthaymin links to the excuse of ignorance for one who never had the truth made clear.

This verse states that God does not forgive associating partners with Him, that He forgives lesser sins to whom He wills, and that whoever associates with God has strayed far astray. Most commentators link its revelation to the case of Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who apostatised and died in idolatry after his theft was exposed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi read it as distinguishing the fate of one who dies as a polytheist from that of other sinners, whose matter rests with God's will. Al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud also record a report from Ibn Abbas about an old Bedouin who confessed his sins but affirmed he never associated anything with God, and Ibn Kathir cites the same tradition. Al-Zamakhshari uses the verse to argue that forgiveness depends on repentance, a view al-Alusi rejects, insisting that the promise of forgiveness for lesser sins stands. All agree that polytheism is the greatest error and the furthest from the right path. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di hold that lesser sins remain under divine will. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi observe that the wording is general and applies to anyone who opposes the path of the believers. Al-Qurtubi also reports that Ali considered it the most beloved verse of the Quran, and that it refutes the Kharijites who held that the grave sinner is a disbeliever.

This verse states that those who abandon God and worship others call upon nothing but females, meaning idols given feminine names such as al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat, and in reality they call upon nothing but a rebellious devil, since their obedience to him in worshipping idols amounts to worshipping him. The commentators agree that the pronoun in 'they call upon' refers to the polytheists and that calling upon means worship here. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi understand 'females' as the idols bearing feminine names, and al-Tabari relies on Aisha's codex, which reads 'idols'. Al-Hasan, Qatada and, in one report, Ibn Abbas take it to mean lifeless objects, since the female is considered lower than the male just as the dead is lower than the living. Al-Dahhak reads it as the angels, whom the pagans called God's daughters. Most identify the devil as Iblis, while Ibn Abbas and Ubayy ibn Ka'b speak of a devil attached to each idol who spoke to the custodians of the shrines. The word 'marid' is explained by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir as the one who is rebellious and persists in disobedience. The commentators also record several readings of 'inathan', such as 'awthanan' or 'wuthunan', without changing the general meaning. Some modern commentaries stress the impotence of these idols, which can benefit no one, and the role of the devil who made their worship seem attractive.

This verse reports that God banished Satan from His mercy, and that Satan swore he would take for himself a fixed, appointed share of God's servants. The commentators explain that a 'prescribed share' means a known or decided portion. Al-Tabari, citing al-Dahhak, says it is a known portion, and Ibn Kathir cites Muqatil that out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine go to Hell and one to Paradise, with al-Qurtubi adding a hadith about the sending forth of the Fire. All agree that Satan secures this share by misleading people, calling them to obey him and making error seem attractive; whoever answers his call belongs to his share. The scholars differ on the 'females' named just before: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada take them to be lifeless objects, Mujahid and Aisha to be idols, al-Dahhak to be the angels, and al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd to be the names al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat. Ibn Abbas held that each idol had a devil speaking to its keepers, while most identify the Satan in question as Iblis himself. On 'altering the creation of God', Ibn Abbas and others understand the religion of God, others understand the castration of animals, and Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan understand tattooing; Ibn Juzayy joins these views, and al-Zamakhshari adds the castration of slaves. The commentators agree that the verse warns against obeying Satan, his false promises and vain hopes, and that whoever takes him as a protector suffers manifest loss.

This passage from Surat al-Nisa' records Satan's oath to lead humans astray. He vows to misguide them from the right path, to deceive them with false hopes, to make them slit the ears of cattle, as the Arabs did with the bahira and the sa'iba to forbid what God had allowed, and to make them alter God's creation. Commentators differ on this last phrase. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and al-Dahhak take it to mean the religion of God, that is, corrupting the original nature, forbidding what is lawful and permitting what is forbidden, citing the verse that there is no changing of God's creation. Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, 'Ikrima and Abu Salih take it to mean castration, which Anas disliked while al-Hasan allowed it for animals. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan in one report take it to mean tattooing, based on the hadith cursing women who tattoo, who pluck their brows, or who file their teeth for beauty. Al-Tabari prefers the view that it means the religion of God, since it covers every disobedience, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi list several forms. As for the end of the verse, the commentators agree that it warns against taking Satan as a protector, and that the clear loss is forfeiting Paradise for the Fire. Ibn Kathir and others add that Satan's promises are only delusion, and that his followers' abode is Hell, from which they will find no escape.

This verse describes the promises and vain hopes with which Satan beguiles his followers, and states that his promises are nothing but deception. The commentators explain that he promises them long life and the fulfilment of their worldly desires, or frightens them with poverty if they give charity, or persuades them that there is no resurrection and no reckoning, so that they take harm for benefit. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi agree that the satanic promise is false and deceptive, and that whoever takes Satan as a protector instead of God has suffered a manifest loss, his refuge being Gehenna. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the promises include what Satan casts into hearts: long life and the hope of escaping punishment while persisting in disobedience. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya widen the meaning of vain desires, citing among them the postponement of repentance and the illusion of intercession. Al-Razi holds that vain desires are the root of misguidance, since greed and hope breed many blameworthy traits, and he defines delusion as thinking something beneficial when its end is harmful. The commentators relate the verse to those who have taken Satan as their master, and see in it a warning against following him, setting God's true promise against Satan's false one.

This part of the verse states that those who took Satan as a protector instead of God, and obeyed him, will have Hell as their abode, and they will find no escape or way out from it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi explain that the word mahis means a place of refuge or a way of escape, from the root meaning to swerve away from something. The commentators link the verse to Satan's threat to his followers: he deceives them with promises and wishful thinking, and their fate is then sealed. They agree that the verse warns against obeying Satan in any act of disobedience, and that whoever follows him suffers a clear loss. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di add that the verse concerns those who submit to Satan and turn away from their Lord. Some, including Ibn Kathir, note that according to Sunni belief sins other than associating partners with God do not bring eternal dwelling in the Fire, a question that is settled by other verses. The warning is followed in the same context by a promise to the righteous believers of gardens with rivers flowing beneath them, to show that wishful thinking is of no use without good deeds, as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

The commentators explain that this verse promises believers who affirm faith in God and His Messenger and do righteous deeds gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will remain forever, and that this is a true promise from God. Al-Tabari holds that righteous deeds mean fulfilling the obligations God has prescribed, and he explains that the emphasis with the words "truly" and "who is more truthful than God in speech" answers the false promise of Satan mentioned in the preceding verses, a view shared by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that qawl and qil have the same meaning. Al-Razi observes that "abadan" (forever) does not necessarily mean endless duration, since the word is also used for long stays, though he does not settle the matter against those who take it as permanence. Ibn Kathir describes the righteous believers as the people of happiness and recounts a report about the companions' fear over the verse on evil deeds. Ibn Juzayy explains that "min" in the following verses marks partial reckoning out of mercy for the servants. Ibn 'Ashur reads the verse as a concluding confirmation of the promise. Al-Sha'rawi highlights the particle "sa", which marks the certainty of the coming event. The commentators agree that the verse pairs warning with promise so that a person holds both fear and hope, and that the closing question is rhetorical, denying that anyone is more truthful than God.

This verse teaches that the reward God promises is not attained through mere wishes, neither those of the Muslims nor those of the People of the Book, but through faith and good deeds. The commentators report that it was revealed when Muslims and People of the Book boasted of their superiority, each claiming to be nearer to God. Whoever does evil will be requited for it, and will find no protector or helper apart from God.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree that the word "evil" (su') covers every sin, great or small, and that the requital may come in this world through trials that expiate sins, as the hadiths cited through Abu Bakr, Aisha and Abu Hurayra report. Al-Hasan al-Basri restricts the threat to the disbeliever, citing the verse "And do We requite any but the ungrateful?" Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take "evil" to mean association with God (shirk). Al-Razi holds that the believer who commits major sins still enters Paradise by the next verse, and that he is punished through lost rewards or the afflictions of this life.

Mujahid states that the address concerns the Quraysh and the Arab polytheists who denied resurrection, while others understand it as addressed to the People of the Book or to Muslims. The following verse makes faith a condition for every good deed and names the finest religion as submitting oneself to God while doing good and following the way of Abraham, whom God took as a friend. Commentators differ on the meaning of "friend" (khalil): some take it as wholehearted love, others as complete dependence on God. None of them resolves the question between these readings.

This verse teaches that Paradise is not reached through wishful thinking but through faith combined with righteous deeds, whether the doer is a man or a woman. Commentators explain that the first "min" in "min al-salihat" is partitive, since no one can perform every good deed, and that faith is a required condition for any deed to be accepted, a point stressed by Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Nasafi. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the pronoun in "wa la yuzlamun" may refer to both those who do evil and those who do good, while al-Razi argues that the denial of any reduction in reward implies, a fortiori, no increase in punishment. The context is the dispute between Muslims, Jews and Christians, each claiming superiority, and the verse settles the matter by the criterion of deeds joined with faith. Ibn Kathir relates the reports of the Companions' distress at the preceding verse, especially Abu Bakr's, and the Prophet's reply that worldly afflictions serve as expiation. On recitation, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr read "yudkhalun" in the passive voice, while the others read it in the active. The naqir is the small mark on the back of a date pit, an image of the utmost smallness.

This verse states that there is no better religion than that of one who submits his face to God while doing good and follows the creed of Abraham, inclining away from falsehood toward monotheism. Commentators explain submitting one's face as sincerity, surrender and reliance on God, and doing good as performing good deeds and avoiding evil, or as worshipping God as though seeing Him. Many take the verse as praising Islam, the religion of Abraham, and some report that it answered the claims of the People of the Book based on the priority of their prophets and scriptures. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi define the hanif as one who turns away from polytheism toward the truth, while al-Razi understands it as one who turns away from all religions. The phrase that God took Abraham as a friend (khalil) is read by most as pure affection and unbroken closeness, though al-Zamakhshari and others offer other etymologies linked to penetrating intimacy or to need. Ibn al-Qayyim holds that this intimate friendship is the highest degree of love and belongs only to Abraham and Muhammad, while others see it as a special election. Ibn Kathir notes that the story of the sand turned into flour cannot be verified. Several commentators also connect the verse to the principle that evil is repaid, with believers expiating their sins in this world, and they differ on the scope of the word evil: Ibn Abbas restricts it to polytheism, while others extend it to all sins.

The commentators explain that this verse, set within a discussion of religion and its people, affirms that everything in the heavens and on earth belongs to God, both in creation and in ownership, and that His knowledge and power encompass all things, so that He repays each person according to their deeds, good or bad. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the encompassing as complete knowledge of everything, nothing escaping Him, not even the weight of an atom. Al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi add that it includes power as well, and see the verse as completing what precedes it on God's oneness and the fulfilment of promises and threats. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud connect it to the mention of righteous doers, noting that obedience to God is owed by the inhabitants of the heavens and earth, so people should choose what is best for themselves. Several scholars, including al-Tabari, al-Nasafi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur, read the phrase as removing any idea that God needs Abraham when He takes him as a close friend, since all creation is His. Al-Razi notes that 'ma' is used rather than 'man' because the sense is generic. The commentators agree that 'kana' does not point to a past time but to the lasting nature of the attribute, and they agree on God's absolute self-sufficiency and the total dependence of creatures on Him. As for the occasion of revelation, Ibn Kathir links it to a dispute between Muslims and People of the Book, but no commentator settles between the differing accounts, and the real disagreements concern the neighbouring verses rather than this one.

Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ about the rights of women, and the answer came that God gives the ruling on them, and also what is recited in the Book concerning orphan women who are not given what was prescribed for them, whom one refuses to marry because they are unattractive, or whom one wishes to marry for their wealth and beauty without fairness. The verse adds the weak young children, who were denied inheritance, and orders guardians to stand by orphans with justice. It ends by stating that God knows whatever good people do. The commentators agree that the verse refers back to the earlier rulings on orphans and inheritance, and that the pre-Islamic society did not give inheritance to women or children. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite the report from 'A'isha, recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim, that a guardian would share his ward's property, wish to marry her or refuse to let another marry her, and so would keep her confined. Al-Tabari, relying on Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Qatada, reports that children and women did not inherit. On the meaning of 'wa targhabuna an tankihuhunna', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as 'you turn away from marrying them because of their plainness', while others, such as al-Hasan and Ibn 'Awn, take it as desire to marry them for their beauty and wealth; al-Tabari favours the first reading. On the grammatical role of 'ma yutla', some link it to God, others to the women, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan weigh several options while finding coordination with the pronoun weak. Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi note that some scholars take the verse as permitting the marriage of a young girl, while the Shafi'is see it as describing a blameworthy pre-Islamic practice. Overall the passage stresses protection of women and the weak and condemns the plundering of orphans' rights.

This verse addresses a couple when first signs of discord appear: a wife fears her husband's aversion or neglect, and it permits the two to reach a settlement, in which she may waive part of her rights, such as some maintenance or her night with him to be given to a co-wife, declaring that reconciliation is better than separation. Commentators cite the case of Sawda bint Zam'a, who gave her turn to 'A'isha, as a common occasion of revelation, while others mention Rafi' ibn Khadij and his wife. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid explained the verse in this sense. Some take the word khawf to mean fear, others knowledge or suspicion. For the phrase that souls are present to stinginess, Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read it as the wife's stinginess towards her husband and his wealth, Ibn Zayd sees it as mutual stinginess between the spouses, and al-Hasan as each holding tightly to his own right. Al-Tabari prefers that it refers to women holding tightly to their rights. The scholars hold that perfect justice between wives in affection and desire is beyond human capacity, which is why the verse forbids leaning wholly toward one so that the other is left as one neither married nor divorced. It closes by reminding that God is fully aware of what people do, and will reward kindness and God-consciousness.

This verse states that a man cannot be perfectly equal among his wives, however hard he tries, because the inclination of the heart, love and intimacy are beyond his control. Ibn Abbas, Ubayda al-Salmani, Mujahid and al-Hasan take the impossible equality to mean equality in love and intimacy, while Ibn Sirin and others limit it to the effort put into love and relations. Hence the prohibition of leaning entirely toward one wife so that the other is left "like one suspended", neither married nor divorced. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi give this meaning, whereas Qatada and Ubayy ibn Ka'b's reading explain it as "imprisoned". Commentators cite the Prophet's ﷺ supplication related by Aisha: "O God, this is my division in what I control; do not blame me for what You control and I do not", which most identify with the heart. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari hold that equity in division, maintenance and good companionship is possible and required. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi transmit the hadith of Abu Hurayra about the man who leans toward one wife and comes on the Day of Resurrection with one side inclined. On the closing phrase, al-Tabari understands forgiveness as covering past lapses through repentance, while al-Zamakhshari sees it as a commitment for the future. The commentators conclude with God's forgiveness and mercy toward what man does not control.

This part of the verse says that if the spouses cannot reconcile and separate, through divorce or otherwise, God promises to enrich each of them from His abundance. He will give the husband a wife better than the one he has left, and the wife a husband more suitable for her, or He will enrich them through contentment and patience. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the separation as divorce, while Ibn 'Atiyya holds that it means physical separation rather than a spoken pronouncement, noting that enrichment comes only after the marital bond has ended. The commentators explain that the abundance (sa'a) means wealth, power and generosity, and that God is vast in His provision, knowledge and mercy. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan note that divorce is permitted but reconciliation is preferable, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that divorce is the most detested of permitted things to God. Ibn Sa'di stresses that God is wise and gives or withholds according to His wisdom. The commentators agree on the general sense of the promise but differ on what the enrichment consists of: some see a new marriage, others inner comfort, and others material wealth.

This verse states that all that is in the heavens and on earth belongs to God alone, and that He enjoined the fear of God on those who were given the Book before you and on you, the community of Muhammad. The commentators explain that piety means worshipping God alone and obeying Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi agree that disbelief does not harm God but only the one who commits it, since God is independent of His creation and praiseworthy in Himself, whether or not He is thanked. They add that the command to be pious is an act of mercy, not a need on God's part. Al-Tabari and al-Nasafi explain that repeating the formula of divine ownership confirms the duty of God-consciousness. Ibn 'Atiyya lists three purposes for the repetition: pointing to the hope of reconciliation, showing God's independence from people, and introducing the warning. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan also discuss the repetition and the readings. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir connect the verse to those who seek only worldly reward: God holds both the reward of this world and of the next, so one should not settle for less. The commentators differ on the warning that God could remove people and bring others in their place. Some apply it to unbelievers and hypocrites, others to humankind in general or to a different kind of creature, as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi report, while al-Tabari ties it to a particular episode of revelation.

The commentators explain that the plain meaning of the verse is that God owns everything in the heavens and on earth, sustains and governs it, and that nothing escapes His knowledge; to take Him as a sufficient guardian (wakil) means to rely on Him alone. This idea recurs in the surrounding verses, and the commentators give different reasons for its repetition. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi see it as emphasis on the duty of piety, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya see it as affirming God's generosity and His independence from creatures. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari also see it as a prelude to the threat of destruction and replacement.

The scholars agree that God has no need of people's obedience and is not harmed by their disbelief, and that the wakil is the one who takes charge of affairs and carries them out as he sees fit; Ibn Kathir adds that He is the watchful witness over everything. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari hold that the command to piety mentioned before applies to all communities and has never been abrogated.

Opinions differ on who is addressed by the warning "He may take you away and bring others". Al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari take it as addressed to the people of the Qur'an or to the Arabs hostile to the Prophet, and they cite the report about Salman al-Farisi; al-Tabari links it to those who defended Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider that the others might not be human, but Abu Hayyan replies that the word "other" implies the same kind. As for "whoever desires the reward of this world", Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari apply it to hypocrites who seek only booty, whereas Ibn Juzayy reads it as a general call to seek the reward of the hereafter too.

The commentators explain that this verse threatens people with destruction and replacement by others should God will it, and affirms that God is fully capable of doing so. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link the passage to the affair of Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who had stolen a coat of mail, and read it as a warning to the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ not to imitate him. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, by contrast, take the address as general to all mankind, and suggest the "others" might even be of a different kind than humans; Abu Hayyan rejects this on linguistic grounds, arguing that the word "other" is only used for something of the same kind as what precedes it. Most commentators, including al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi, identify those addressed as the polytheists and hypocrites, with the replacements described as more obedient to God. Several report that when the verse was revealed the Prophet ﷺ struck Salman's back and said they are the people of this man, meaning the Persians, a report cited by al-Tabari, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi. Others, such as Ibn Sa'di and Sayyid Qutb, read it as a general warning against disobedience. Al-Shinqiti and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress God's absolute power to annihilate and create, noting that the closing phrase on His power emphasises this. None of these scholars settles the matter in favour of one reading over the others.

The commentators explain that the verse concerns the person whose actions aim only at worldly rewards. It states that the reward of this world and of the Hereafter both belong to God, so whoever is content with worldly gain alone has lowered his aim, since God owns both. Al-Tabari understands it as referring to the hypocrites who displayed faith to obtain booty and to secure their lives, property and families, while their reward in the Hereafter is the Fire; he supports this with a verse from Hud. Al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi, al-Nasafi and others read it as referring to the fighter who seeks only spoils: whoever fights sincerely for God will not miss the spoils, and he has in the Hereafter a reward compared to which the spoils are nothing. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya see a condition and a warning against seeking only worldly profit. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi report that Arab polytheists drew near to God for worldly goods without believing in resurrection, and God tells them that the good of both worlds is with Him. Ibn Kathir holds that God gives both to whoever asks Him for both, and he criticises Tabari's reading. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi take the answer to the condition to be implied, namely that one should seek both rewards from God. Finally, the closing words 'God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing' are generally taken as both a warning and a promise: God hears the words and sees the intentions, and rewards each according to his aim.

This verse commands believers to stand firmly for justice and bear witness for God alone, even against themselves, their parents or their relatives, whether the party concerned is rich or poor, since God is more worthy of caring for them than they are. The commentators explain that testifying against oneself means acknowledging the truth, as al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note. They agree that neither the wealth of the one testified against nor pity for the poor should sway the witness. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir stress that the verse concerns honest testimony. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi hold that the pronoun 'bihima' refers to the categories of rich and poor rather than to two particular persons. On the phrase 'do not follow your desires lest you deviate from justice', al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy read it as a warning against turning away from what is right, while others take it as fear of straying. Regarding 'if you distort or refuse', the dominant reading is that the witness twists or withholds testimony, though Ibn 'Ashur notes the phrase may also describe a judge bending a ruling. Al-Qurtubi reports that jurists drew from the verse rules on whether a child's testimony for or against parents, or a spouse's testimony for a spouse, is admissible, and the opinions differ. The verse closes with a warning that God is aware of what people do.

This verse calls the believers to strengthen their faith and remain steadfast in it, commanding them to believe in God, His Messenger Muhammad, the Quran revealed to him, and the Scriptures revealed before him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and others address the believers and read the command as an exhortation to persevere and remain firm, not as an order to acquire what is already held. Al-Mawardi notes that the address may be to the People of the Book, if faith in earlier prophets is meant, or to the hypocrites, if inner faith is meant; al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi also record these readings, while al-Hasan al-Basri takes it as a call to steadfastness and Mujahid sees the hypocrites in view. Several commentators, including al-Wahidi, al-Tha'alibi and Ibn Kathir, report that the verse was revealed about 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions among the People of the Book, who wished to believe only in the Torah and Moses, and who then accepted belief in all of it.

The commentators agree that the first Book is the Quran and that the second is a generic term covering the Torah, the Gospel and all earlier scriptures. They hold that belief in the Books means accepting those that are authentic, and that rejecting any one element of faith amounts to rejecting all of them, as Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Ibn Sa'di state. Al-Razi explains that the order in which prophets and Books are mentioned follows either the descent of revelation or its ascent. Ibn 'Uthaymin draws from the verse that the Quran is the last of the Books. The phrase 'far astray' is explained by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir as a deviation so distant from the straight path that there is no return from it.

This verse describes people who believed, then renounced their faith, then believed again, then disbelieved once more, and finally grew in disbelief, so that God will neither forgive them nor guide them to a path of salvation. The commentators disagree on who they are. Qatada and Abu al-'Aliya, whom al-Tabari favours, identify them as Jews and Christians: the Jews believed in the Torah and then rejected it, the Christians believed in the Gospel and then rejected it, and then both rejected Muhammad. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd identify them as hypocrites who oscillated between faith and unbelief until they died in hypocrisy, a view also recorded by Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir. Al-Hasan speaks of a group among the People of the Book who showed faith to unsettle the Muslims, and Ibn 'Abbas extends the meaning to every hypocrite of the Prophet's time. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand the negation as a statement of how unlikely a sound, lasting faith is for people whose hearts have hardened through repeated apostasy, not as a claim that repentance would be refused. Al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the lam here expresses the negation of God's will. On the legal question, Ali, as cited by al-Tabari, holds that an apostate should be asked to repent three times, while others, including al-Shafi'i according to al-Mawardi, say he is asked each time he apostatises. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir observe that repentance is generally accepted, and that the verse mainly describes the end of those who persist.

God instructs His Prophet to tell the hypocrites, those who show faith outwardly while concealing disbelief, that a painful punishment awaits them. The word "give good news" is used ironically, since it normally signals something pleasant, and commentators take it as a mockery of them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that this punishment is the Fire of Hell, and that it is painful. According to al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan, the hypocrites sided with disbelievers, especially Jews, seeking strength and dominance over the Muslims, and God replies that all power belongs to Him. The commentators also agree that verse 137, about those who repeatedly believe and then disbelieve, refers in many views to the hypocrites: Mujahid and Ibn Zayd describe them as repeatedly disbelieving until death, while al-Hasan and Qatada see it as referring to People of the Book. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan report several opinions. On the meaning of the denial of forgiveness, the majority, including al-Razi and al-Alusi, understand it as the absence of a sincere and lasting faith, while others take it to mean that they die in disbelief. The commentators also draw from this passage a prohibition on sitting with those who mock God's verses: Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Shawkani treat it as a lasting rule, while Ibn Kathir reports that Muqatil considered it abrogated by another verse, a view al-Shawkani rejects.

This verse describes hypocrites who take disbelievers as allies instead of believers and seek power and strength from them. God replies that all might belongs to Him alone, and He grants it to whom He wills among His servants. The commentators agree that the hypocrites are the subject, and that the disbelievers were mainly the Jews; al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that these hypocrites relied on them and said to one another that Muhammad's affair would not succeed. Ibn 'Abbas specifies the Banu Qaynuqa, with whom Ibn Ubayy allied. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the word 'bashshir' (announce good news) is used ironically to announce punishment. The word 'izza' means strength, power and domination, and its root is the idea of hard ground, as al-Wahidi, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya note. Al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi read the question as a rebuke, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di take it as a call to seek strength from God and to ally with believers. On who the disbelievers are, al-Tabari and Abu Hayyan name the Jews and Christians, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Shawkani also include the polytheists of Mecca. The second part of the verse, forbidding sitting with those who mock God's signs, is linked by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to Surat al-An'am; Muqatil considers it abrogated, whereas most commentators hold the prohibition still valid.

This verse recalls that God has already revealed in the Book, as stated in Surat al-An'am, that when believers hear God's signs being denied and mocked, they should not sit with those who do so until they turn to other talk, because sitting with them in that state makes the sitter one of them in sin. It also announces that God will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers together in Hell. The commentators agree that the address is to those who profess faith, and that the hypocrites meant were groups who sat with Jewish rabbis and mocked the Quran, while the Muslims in Mecca had been told to avoid polytheists who did the same. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir treat the ruling as firm, as do al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur, whereas al-Kalbi held it abrogated by the verse 'Nothing of their reckoning falls on those who fear God'; al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur reject this. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi extend the prohibition to all people of innovation and sin, and al-Qurtubi cites al-Dahhak saying it covers every innovator in religion until the Day of Judgment. On the nature of the likeness, opinions differ: some place it in disobedience, others in approval of disbelief. Al-Razi holds that whoever approves of disbelief is a disbeliever, but one who sits unwillingly under compulsion is not. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan report that 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz had men who drank wine flogged and recited this verse when told one of them was fasting. On the phrase 'God will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers', 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas referred it to the Hereafter, while others understood it as a proof or a lasting victory.

This verse describes hypocrites who wait to see what befalls the believers. If the Muslims win a victory and booty, they say, "Were we not with you?", seeking a share of the spoils; if the disbelievers gain an advantage, they tell them, "Did we not gain control over you and shield you from the believers?" God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection, and He will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers. Commentators explain that istihwadh means to dominate and take control. They differ on the meaning of the protection claimed: al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as discouraging the believers and presenting a favour, al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya as passing on information and weakening the believers, and al-Zamakhshari as undermining their resolve. All agree that the Muslims' victory is called fath to honour them, while the disbelievers' share is called nasib to belittle it. Regarding the "way" denied to the disbelievers, al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir report, following 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, that it refers to the Day of Judgement, while al-Sudi takes it to mean proof, and others mean total domination. The exegetes also note that the hypocrites enjoyed the outward benefits of Islam in this world, including a share of the spoils.

This verse describes hypocrites who try to deceive God by showing faith while concealing disbelief, and God deals with them as one who outwits a deceiver, leaving them in their delusion in this world and preparing the lowest level of Hell for them. The commentators agree that when they stand for prayer they do so lazily, as if compelled, hoping for no reward and fearing no punishment, and that they pray only to be seen by people so that they appear to be believers. Their remembrance of God is scarce. Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan explain that this is because they act for other than God; Qatada says God did not accept their remembrance, so what is rejected is little, while others take it to mean prayer or only the takbir and silent formulas. Regarding the divine deception in the hereafter, al-Hasan, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj report that God gives the hypocrites a light on the bridge and then extinguishes it, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as God leaving them safe in this life and reserving the lowest depth of Fire for them. On the phrase wavering between that, most take it as hesitation between faith and disbelief, belonging to neither the believers nor the unbelievers, with differences in reading and etymology. Some, such as Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, cite the hadith of the goat wavering between two flocks, and Ibn Kathir adds the report that the hypocrite watches the sun before praying four quick rak'ahs.

This verse describes the hypocrites as wavering between faith and disbelief, belonging neither to the believers nor to the disbelievers, and states that whomever God misguides has no path to guidance. The commentators explain that tadhabdhub means agitation and oscillation: the hypocrite is confused in his religion and holds to no sound belief, being neither truly with the believers nor with the polytheists in ignorance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi agree that the hypocrites show faith to the believers while concealing disbelief, Ibn Kathir stating that their outward side is with the believers and their inner side with the disbelievers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir transmit from Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd that these people are neither sincere believers nor open polytheists, with Mujahid adding that they are not with the Prophet's companions nor with the Jews. Al-Tabari cites the hadith of Ibn Umar about the goat wavering between two flocks, which he judges to have a sound chain, and Ibn Kathir adds the story of the three men at a river attributed to the Prophet. Al-Zamakhshari explains that Satan and desire push such people between faith and unbelief so they never settle on one side. As for the final clause, al-Tabari understands it as one whom God leaves without help toward the right path, which is Islam, while al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn take it simply as having no way to guidance. Ibn Abbas read the second dhal with a kasra, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read it with a ta', readings that the commentators say do not significantly change the meaning.

In this verse God forbids the believers to take disbelievers as close allies and supporters in place of fellow believers, warning that doing so would give God a clear proof against them for their punishment. The commentators agree that the address is first to the believers and that the prohibition covers affection, support, trust and reliance on disbelievers, and that whoever does this resembles the hypocrites described just before. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya read sultan as proof, relying on Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and Mujahid, who said that every sultan in the Quran means proof. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan also mention the sense of power and domination. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see such alliance as clear evidence of hypocrisy. Al-Wahidi reports that the verse was revealed concerning the Ansar and their ties with the Banu Qurayza, while al-Razi holds that it targets alliance with the hypocrites. On the lowest level of the Fire reserved for hypocrites, readers differ over the vowelling of the letter ra', and the commentators agree that their punishment is heavier than that of disbelievers, since they combine unbelief with mockery and betrayal of the Muslims. Ibn Mas'ud describes them locked in closed iron coffins within the Fire. All agree that repentance is accepted on condition of reforming conduct, holding fast to God and purifying the faith, which joins them to the believers. Finally, the commentators explain that God does not punish the grateful believer, His gratitude being the reward He grants even for a little good deed.

This verse states that the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of Hell, the most severe place of punishment, and that no one will be found to save them. The commentators explain that daraka means a level or stage, and they agree that Hell has stacked levels, with the hypocrite at the very bottom. The two readings, with the letter ra vowelled or unvowelled, are both accepted as correct and carry the same meaning, though some prefer the vowelled form as more common in Arabic and more usual in the plural. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayra, reported by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, say the lowest level consists of closed iron coffins in which the fire burns. To explain why their punishment is so severe, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the hypocrite adds mockery of Islam and deceit of the believers to disbelief, which makes him worse than the open unbeliever. Al-Razi adds that because the hypocrite learns the secrets of the Muslims and passes them to the unbelievers, his trial is doubled. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite Ibn 'Umar's saying that the people who suffer most on the Day of Resurrection are the hypocrites, the unbelievers among the people of the table, and the family of Pharaoh, and al-Razi observes that this does not contradict the verse in Ghafir since the lowest level holds both groups. The verses that follow open the door of repentance: most commentators hold that whoever repents, reforms, holds fast to God and makes his religion sincere joins the believers, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir add that even a small sincere action is enough. Al-Zamakhshari defines hypocrisy as showing faith while concealing disbelief, and sees in the term's use for sinners a way of strongly rebuking them.

This verse states that the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire, with no one to rescue them. It then opens the door of repentance to those who turn back, on four conditions: repenting from hypocrisy, correcting what they had spoiled, holding fast to God, and making their religion sincere for Him. Whoever meets these conditions is counted among the believers and will receive their great reward. The commentators explain that the lowest level is the deepest tier of hellfire, and that the hypocrite suffers a harsher punishment because his hypocrisy adds mockery of Islam and deceit toward its people to disbelief. On the reading, the Kufans read "al-darki" with a silent r, while others vocalize it; Abu Ali sees two equivalent dialects, and some prefer the vocalized form because its plural is adrak. Al-Farra' explains that "with the believers" means "among the believers", while al-Qutaybi holds that the wording avoids calling them believers out of anger at their hypocrisy. Some commentators report that a group of hypocrites will enter Paradise after repenting, as Hudhayfa related. Scholars differ on whether the hypocrite's repentance is accepted: some reject it, while others accept it once his sincerity is established. The commentators conclude that God has no need to punish His servants and does not punish the grateful believer.

The commentators explain that this verse is phrased as a question meant to deny: what would God gain by punishing you if you thank Him for His favours and believe in Him? God, who is self-sufficient, neither benefits from obedience nor is harmed by disobedience; punishment follows from disbelief and hypocrisy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi agree that God does not punish the grateful believer, that gratitude means acknowledging a favour and obeying its Giver, and that God's gratitude means reward and acceptance. They differ on the order of the terms. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that a person first feels a general gratitude and then believes in the Benefactor, whereas Abu Hayyan and Ibn Atiyya hold that true gratitude necessarily includes faith and that it is mentioned for emphasis, while some treat the order as a case of inversion. Ibn Abbas understood gratitude here as monotheism. Ibn al-Qayyim draws from the verse that God's gratitude rules out punishing His servants without cause and neglecting the good deeds of the righteous. The verse follows the description of the hypocrites, who are in the lowest level of the Fire, with the exception of those who repent sincerely. Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi note that the verse presents gratitude and faith as the way to salvation, God accepting even small deeds and multiplying their reward.

This verse from Surah al-Nisa' says that God does not love the public utterance of evil speech, and it makes an exception for the person who has been wronged. The most common reading, "illa man zulima", meaning "except one who has been wronged", is accepted by the commentators, who agree that the exception allows the victim to complain and to speak of the harm done to him. They differ on how far this may go. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, holds that the wronged person may call down harm on his oppressor, though patience is better. Al-Hasan al-Basri says he may pray, "O God, help me against him and restore my right", without exceeding the limit. Mujahid understood the verse as concerning a guest who has been poorly received, who may publicly describe his treatment; al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi favour this reading. Al-Sudi holds that the victim may retaliate with an equivalent wrong. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that this permission does not extend to slander. The alternative reading, "illa man zalama", attributed to Ibn Zayd and several early readers, refers to one who persists in hypocrisy and is to be rebuked to his face; al-Zamakhshari reads it as an oppressor who insults others. The verse closes with God's hearing and knowledge, then urges doing good, openly or in secret, and pardoning wrongs, since God pardons even though He is able to punish.

This verse says that God does not love the public utterance of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged, who may complain of his oppressor or call down a curse upon him. It then urges believers to do good, whether openly or in secret, and to pardon those who have wronged them, noting that God pardons His servants though He has full power to punish them. The commentators agree on the principle that speaking ill openly is blameworthy and that the wronged person is an exception. They differ on what that exception permits. Al-Hasan al-Basri says it is a prayer such as 'O God, help me against him and restore my right,' while Ibn 'Abbas allows invoking a curse against the oppressor, and Mujahid links it to a guest who was poorly received and complains of it. Al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas also allow retaliation with a matching wrong. Ibn Kathir cites hadiths permitting the complaint, and some scholars drew from them an obligation of hospitality. Al-Zamakhshari, reading one way, takes the exception as referring to the oppressor who speaks evil, while Ibn Zayd applies the verse to hypocrites who are to be rebuked. Almost all agree that pardoning while able to punish is the higher virtue. Al-Razi reduces all good to conveying benefit and averting harm, which covers both giving and forgiving. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the verse mentions speech because it is the least harmful form of injury.

This verse addresses those who disbelieve in God and His messengers among the People of the Book. Most commentators identify them as Jews and Christians: the Jews believed in Moses and the Torah but rejected Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them, while the Christians believed in Jesus but rejected Muhammad ﷺ. They wish to separate belief in God from belief in His messengers, accepting some prophets and rejecting others, and imagine a middle path between faith and disbelief. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud hold that no such middle path exists, since faith in God is complete only when one believes in all His messengers, so rejecting one amounts to rejecting all. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi add that this stance springs from whim and partisanship rather than from evidence.

The commentators broadly agree that the word "truly" confirms their disbelief is complete and certain. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi note that partial faith benefits them nothing. As for the humiliating punishment, al-Tabari explains it as an everlasting torment in the Fire that disgraces those who suffer it, and Ibn Kathir sees it as a recompense for their arrogance.

Al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi report that the passage was revealed in the context of Jewish demands that the Prophet ﷺ bring down a book from heaven. Al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi interpret the "middle path" as a religion lying between Judaism and Islam. Ibn Kathir concludes by contrasting these people with the believers, the community of Muhammad ﷺ, who believe in all books and all prophets without distinction and to whom God promises reward, forgiveness and mercy.

This verse states that whoever believes in God but rejects His messengers, or believes in some prophets and rejects others, is a disbeliever in truth. Most commentators apply it to Jews and Christians. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Suddi report that the Jews believed in Moses and the Torah but rejected Jesus and Muhammad, while the Christians believed in Jesus and rejected Muhammad; this separation between the prophets is a separation between God and His messengers. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan hold that rejecting one messenger amounts to rejecting all of them, since the proof that establishes one prophet's truth applies equally to the others, and faith cannot be divided. Al-Zamakhshari reads the phrase about a middle path as a religion lying between belief and disbelief, which he rejects because there is no middle ground. Some understand it as an invented faith between Judaism and Islam. Regarding the word haqqan, most take it as emphasis on the sentence, meaning a firm and certain disbelief; al-Wahidi objected to this grammatical reading, but the majority answered that the sense is completeness and certainty rather than the opposite of falsehood. On the humiliating punishment, al-Tabari and al-Baydawi explain that it will degrade those who suffer it in the hereafter. Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Jaza'iri note that repeating the noun 'the disbelievers' instead of using a pronoun gives the statement generality and signals the reason for the judgment, namely disbelief. Ibn 'Ashur adds that this passage answers the similar verses in Surat al-Baqara and Al 'Imran.

This verse promises that those who believe in God and all His messengers, without distinguishing between them by accepting some and rejecting others, will be given their reward, and that God is Forgiving and Merciful toward them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it to refer to the community of Muhammad ﷺ, who believe in every scripture and every prophet sent by God; Ibn Juzayy reads it the same way. For al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, not distinguishing means accepting all the messengers as truthful in what they brought; al-Tabari adds that it excludes calling some of them liars and others truthful. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi note that the word "ahad" can cover two people or more because it is general. Al-Razi draws from the verse that true faith is not nullified by sins, and al-Nasafi sees in it a rebuttal of the Mu'tazilites on the eternal punishment of the grave sinner. Ibn 'Ashur links the verse to others that forbid separating the messengers, and says that separating them amounts to separating God from some of them. Al-Qasimi and Ibn 'Uthaymin explain that the prohibited distinction concerns the core of faith, not the revealed law, which differs between eras; Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that ranking the prophets, based on the text, is permitted, provided it does not lead to dispute.

This verse reports that the People of the Book, chiefly the Jews, asked the Prophet ﷺ to bring down a written book from heaven to them. The commentators give several readings of this request. Al-Sudi and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi take it to mean a book written down, like the Torah given to Moses. Qatada and al-Hasan see a demand made out of obstinacy and for their own sake alone, while Ibn Jurayj reports that they wanted letters sent to named individuals confirming his prophethood. Al-Tabari concludes that it was a written miracle sent down to their community, while recognising other possibilities. Most agree that the request was made in defiance rather than seeking guidance, as al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di emphasise.

The verse then gives an example from their own history: they asked Moses for something greater, saying, "Show us God openly," and the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing; then they took the calf as a god after clear signs had come to them. Commentators agree that this is both a rebuke and a consolation for the Prophet. They differ on the meaning of "openly": al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as direct sight, whereas, according to Ibn 'Abbas as reported by al-Tabari, it qualifies the speech rather than the seeing. On the wrongdoing involved, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir see it as obstinacy and the demand itself, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya see it in the request to see God; al-Razi and Abu Hayyan reply that seeing God is possible in the afterlife.

The pardon granted to the worshippers of the calf after their repentance, and the "clear authority" given to Moses, which is the evidence he brought, are explained in agreement by al-Jalalayn, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi.

This verse tells how God raised Mount Tur above the Children of Israel because of their covenant, meaning because they had refused to act on what was in the Torah until they feared and accepted it. He commanded them to enter the gate of Jerusalem prostrating, not to transgress on the Sabbath, and took from them a solemn covenant. The commentators differ on some details. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that Tur is the mountain itself, and that it was raised when they refused to accept the Torah. Al-Tabari, following Qatada, says the gate is one of the gates of the Bayt al-Maqdis, while others name the gate of Hitta, Ilya or Ariha. On the prostration, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya report that they entered crawling on their buttocks, whereas Ibn Ashur reads it as a prostration of thanks for the conquest. On the prohibition of transgressing on the Sabbath, al-Tabari explains it as the prohibition of catching fish on that day. The recitations differ: Warsh, transmitted from Nafi, reads with a fatha on the ain and a doubled dal, while the others read it differently. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir report that the transgression took the form of a trick, which brought them punishment. Most commentators take the solemn covenant to be a strengthened pledge, though some see it as a sworn oath; Ibn Ashur explains that the word "solemn" refers to the strength of the commitment. Ibn Kathir and others conclude that the Children of Israel broke their pledges and that God punished them by forbidding them some good things.

The commentators explain that this verse lists the offences for which the Children of Israel were cursed: breaking their covenant, rejecting God's signs, killing the prophets unjustly, and saying 'our hearts are wrapped in coverings'. Al-Tabari explains that 'ghulf' means hearts covered by envelopes that prevent them from understanding what the Prophet says; God refutes this claim and says that He sealed their hearts because of their disbelief, so they believe only a little. Ibn Abbas and others understand 'ghulf' as containers of knowledge that need nothing beyond what they hold. Al-Zajjaj reads the sealing as a statement carrying blame. Scholars also differ on what the phrase 'fa-bima' is connected to. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir assume an implied verb, 'We cursed them', while al-Zamakhshari and al-Zajjaj link it to 'We forbade them good things', making that prohibition a consequence of their misdeeds. Ibn Kathir notes that 'qalilan' may mean either a weak faith or a small number of believers, and Ibn Abbas identifies that small number with Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions. The commentaries agree that the verse lists the sins that cost the Children of Israel guidance, and that a faith professed only when death is seen brings no benefit.

This part of the verse states that the Jews deserved the curse because of their disbelief, including their rejection of Jesus and their accusation against Mary of adultery, which the verse calls a great slander. The commentators explain that the gravity of the charge lay partly in the fact that it was made despite the signs that had appeared to prove Mary's innocence. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi, citing Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and others, read the word as the accusation of fornication. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy agree and add that the repetition of the word disbelief stresses the seriousness of their sin. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the repetition shows that the Jews rejected Moses, then Jesus, then Muhammad in succession, and that the phrase refers to the whole set of their faults. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi observe that the conjunction may link this disbelief to the faults before it. Al-Qurtubi reports a view that links the slander to the story of Yusuf the carpenter. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Ashur note that the accusation contradicted Mary's known purity. These explanations agree on the essential point: the slander against Mary is a grave sin, and it joins the other faults listed in the passage to explain the curse.

The commentators explain that this part of the verse rejects the claim of the Jews that they killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God. God states that they neither killed him nor crucified him, but that his likeness was cast upon another man in their eyes. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Wahidi report the widely known account that Jesus's likeness was placed on one of his companions or on the man who had guided the Jews to him; they killed and crucified that man believing him to be Jesus, while Jesus was raised alive to heaven. Some report that the likeness fell only on the face, and this point has been disputed. As for the phrase about those who differed concerning him being in doubt, most understand it to mean that the Jews and Christians disagreed about the identity of the slain man, lacking knowledge and following only conjecture. The word translated as certainty may refer to the killing, to the killers' state of mind, or to the negation itself, and the exegetes differ in which sense they adopt. Finally, the statement that every People of the Book will believe in him before his death is taken by most to refer to Jesus at his descent near the end of time, while some understood it as a faith at the moment of death that brings no benefit. These matters remain debated among the scholars.

This passage states that God raised Jesus, son of Mary, up to Himself: he was neither killed nor crucified, and the Jews who claimed to have killed him had no certainty, since the likeness was confused for them and they killed another man. The commentators report that the accounts differ on how this happened. According to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid, Wahb ibn Munabbih and al-Sudi, Jesus's likeness was cast upon one of his companions, or upon a man who had shown the Jews where he was hiding; they crucified and killed him thinking he was the Messiah, while Jesus was raised alive. Al-Tabari, following one version from Wahb, notes that the likeness was cast on all the disciples; al-Jubba'i saw a confusion that the Jewish leaders had deliberately maintained to calm the people. As for 'they did not kill him with certainty', Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sudi take it to mean they did not make their assumption a reality, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba relate it to knowledge, and al-Hasan reads it as 'truly'. Most say Jesus was raised to heaven, others to a place where no one's judgement applies but God's. In the next verse, most exegetes, including Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Malik, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, take the pronoun in 'before his death' to refer to Jesus: no People of the Book will remain who do not believe in him before his death, at his descent at the end of time. Others, such as al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak, take it to refer to the individual of the People of the Book at the moment of dying, whose faith then does not benefit him; 'Ikrima also reads it as referring to Muhammad. Finally, 'he will be a witness against them on the Day of Resurrection': according to Qatada and Ibn Jurayj, Jesus will testify that he conveyed his Lord's message; according to others, he will accuse the Jews of rejecting him and the Christians of exaggerating about him.

This verse states that none of the People of the Book will remain who does not believe in Jesus before his death, and that Jesus will be a witness against them on the Day of Resurrection. The commentators differ on what the pronouns refer to. Ibn 'Abbas and most early authorities, including Abu Malik, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan, hold that both pronouns refer to Jesus: every People of the Book will believe in him when he descends at the end of time, before his own death, and all religions will then become one, the religion of Islam. Al-Tabari adopts this view as the most correct and relies on the hadith of Abu Hurayra about Jesus's descent and his forty years on earth. By contrast, 'Ikrima, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan take the first pronoun to refer to Jesus and the second to the individual People of the Book: each one, at the moment of death, when the truth becomes clear to him, will affirm faith in Jesus, but this faith will not benefit him. Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have said that a Jew will speak the profession even if his neck is struck or he falls from a roof, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b's reading "before their death" is cited in support. Some report that the pronoun refers to the Prophet Muhammad, a view ascribed to 'Ikrima and considered weak by several scholars since he is not mentioned in the verse. As for the witness on the Day of Judgment, Qatada and Ibn Jurayj understand it as Jesus attesting that he delivered his Lord's message and acknowledged his servitude, while others take it as testimony against the Jews for their denial and against the Christians for their exaggeration.

This verse explains that God forbade the Jews certain good things that had been lawful to them, as a punishment for their wrongdoing and for their turning many people, and themselves, away from God's path. The commentators agree that this wrongdoing includes breaking the covenant, rejecting God's signs, killing the prophets and slandering Mary, and that the prohibition was a punishment. Most identify the forbidden good things with those mentioned in Surat al-An'am: every animal with undivided hooves and the fat of cattle and sheep. Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have read the phrase as 'good things which had been permitted', which indicates they were lawful before. As for turning away from God's path, al-Tabari, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan take it to mean turning many people away, while others take it to mean turning themselves away from the truth. Usury and consuming people's wealth by falsehood, such as bribery, are also sins they had been forbidden. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir link these sins to what precedes them. Al-Shinqiti and Ibn 'Uthaymin note that the prohibition may be a legal ruling or a decreed consequence. Ibn al-Qayyim draws from the verse a ban on treating illness with forbidden substances, while al-Qurtubi uses it to argue for permitting dealings with the People of the Book. The following verses, which except the firm in knowledge among them, are linked by the commentators to Abdullah ibn Salam and his like. They also differ on the grammar of 'the establishers of prayer', between accusative of praise according to Sibawayh and coordination according to others.

This verse explains that the Jews were punished for their wrongdoing: God forbade them certain good things that had been lawful for them, because of their frequent turning people away from God's way, their taking of usury although they had been forbidden it, and their wrongful consumption of other people's wealth. Commentators agree that these faults belonged to the Jews of that time, and that the painful punishment is reserved for those among them who disbelieved. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others see the prohibition as a legal penalty, the forbidden good things being, according to the chapter of the Cattle, every animal with undivided hooves and the fat of cattle and sheep. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take the injustice as a term covering their earlier sins, such as breaking the covenant and killing the prophets. Turning people from God's path is understood by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy as turning oneself and others away from the truth through rejecting Muhammad and distorting the Book, while some take it simply as refusal of faith. Regarding usury, al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi define it as an increase over the principal in exchange for a delay, and the wrongful eating of wealth includes bribery and the price of falsified books. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-'Arabi hold that the verse does not forbid dealing with People of the Book, such dealings remaining permitted. The following exception is explained by most as referring to 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and those who converted, with the believers alongside them being those among the People of the Book who believed, or the Emigrants and Helpers. Grammarians differ on the case of the phrase 'those who establish the prayer': Sibawayh takes it as an accusative of praise, followed by al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, others link it to what precedes it, and some report that 'A'isha and Aban ibn 'Uthman considered it a scribal error, a view rejected by al-Tabari and Abu Hayyan.

This verse makes an exception for the firmly rooted scholars among the People of the Book, those whose knowledge is settled and certain, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions, after the preceding verses have described Jewish wrongdoing, usury and the devouring of people's wealth in falsehood. The commentators explain that these believers accept the Quran revealed to the Prophet and the earlier scriptures, perform the prayer, give zakat, believe in God and the Last Day, and that God promises them a great reward, which al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take to be Paradise. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi identify these scholars with Jews who embraced Islam, while al-Zamakhshari extends the term to the believers among them, or to the believing Emigrants and Helpers. The main disagreement concerns the grammar of 'al-muqimin al-salah'. Sibawayh and al-Zamakhshari take it as an accusative of praise that highlights the importance of prayer. Al-Kisa'i and al-Tabari treat it as a genitive linked to 'ma' in 'what was sent down to you', so that it means the angels for al-Tabari and al-Mubarrad, or the prophets for al-Kisa'i. A view attributed to Aisha and Aban ibn Uthman calls the form a scribal error; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi reject it, and al-Nahhas judges the accusative of praise the soundest explanation. Ibn Kathir and the Jalalayn note that 'al-mu'tun' is in the nominative as a new clause. Hamza reads the verb in the third person, 'yu'tihim', while the rest read it in the first person.

God tells His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that He revealed to him as He revealed to Noah and the prophets after him, and to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon, and that He gave David the Zabur. The point is that the revelation given to the Prophet is not unprecedented among the messengers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the verse answers Jews who claimed God had sent no revelation to any human after Moses, and some connect it to their demand that a book be sent down from heaven. The commentators agree that revelation is a swift and hidden communication, that Noah was the first messenger, and that monotheism is the common core of what all the messengers received, while the laws differ between peoples, as Ibn Uthaymin notes. On the word Zabur, the majority reading with a fatha names the book itself, while Hamza reads it with a damma as a plural meaning written scriptures. Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya prefer the first reading. Several scholars hold that God truly spoke to Moses without intermediary, and Ibn Kathir considers denying this a distortion. The exegetes note that some prophets are not named in the Qur'an and that their number cannot be fixed with certainty, though the hadith of Abu Dhar on the subject is judged weak by Ibn Kathir. Ibn Kathir also stresses that Muhammad's mission is not unprecedented, and that the sending of messengers serves to leave people no excuse before God on the Day of Judgment.

This passage affirms that the revelation given to Muhammad ﷺ is of the same kind as that given to earlier prophets, so there is no ground for the Jews to object that he should receive revelation at all. Commentators explain that God sent messengers whose stories He related in the Quran, and others whose stories He did not relate. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the numbers reported in hadith are not firmly established, and that it is better to rely on what the Quran states. All agree that the purpose of sending messengers as bringers of good news and warners is to remove any excuse people might offer on the Day of Judgment. Grammarians differ on how to parse the word rusulan: some take it as object of an implied verb such as we sent, others link it to what precedes, and Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi offer further readings. On the clause that God spoke to Moses with direct speech, the majority take it as proof that God's speech is real and not figurative, and that the address was direct and without an intermediary. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir cite it against those who say God created a sound in an object, or who read the verb as meaning to wound; al-Razi and al-Shawkani likewise reject those readings. Ibn Kathir however notes that accounts describing the nature of that voice, transmitted from Ka'b al-Ahbar, are not authentic. The common conclusion is that revelation was shared by all the prophets, and that Moses was singled out for a direct conversation with God.
