The commentators explain that this verse means God sent messengers as bringers of good news to those who obey and as warners to those who disobey, so that people would have no excuse before God after they were sent. Al-Tabari says the aim is to cut off the argument of one who would say, had a messenger come to me I would have believed. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that sending the messengers removes the excuse and reminds people of what reason alone cannot fully establish, such as the details of worship and law. The Mu'tazilites maintain that reason suffices to know God and to make knowledge obligatory before revelation, and they read the verse as merely awakening people to what reason already requires. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya draw from it that God does not punish people before a messenger is sent, and al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report that knowledge of God is established only through revelation. The commentators differ on the number of prophets and messengers: Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith of Abu Dharr without fully vouching for it, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers the figure unsound. All agree that God's might means nothing overpowers Him, and that His wisdom means His acts proceed from perfect knowledge, including not granting the demands of those who seek to obstruct. Al-Shinqiti points to the verses of Ta-Ha and al-Qasas to clarify this excuse, and Ibn 'Uthaymin concludes that God loves to accept excuses, and that ignorance may excuse unless it stems from neglect in seeking knowledge.

This verse states that God Himself bears witness to the revelation sent to the Prophet ﷺ, answering those who refused to acknowledge his mission. God testifies that the Qur'an He sent down to him is from Him, sent down with His knowledge, and the angels also bear witness, yet God's witness alone is sufficient. The commentators read the opening 'but' as a response to those who refuse to testify for the Prophet. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari take God's witness to mean the manifestation of miracles that establish the truth of a claim, just as claims are proven by evidence. On the phrase 'sent it down with His knowledge', opinions differ: al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi read it as 'sent it down containing His knowledge', al-Tabari as 'with knowledge from Him that you are His chosen one', al-Zamakhshari as the inimitable arrangement of its wording that no eloquent speaker can match, and Ibn Kathir as the presence in it of knowledge of the unseen and of divine laws. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir see in the phrase a proof, for the Sunnis, that God has knowledge, against the Mu'tazila. The angels' witness is understood by al-Razi and al-Nasafi as their acknowledgment of the mission once the miraculous proof is established, and by Ibn al-Jawzi as a testimony that the Qur'an was sent down or to the Prophet's truthfulness. Several commentators, including al-Baydawi, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur, note that the closing phrase does not make the angels' testimony necessary, but recalls that God alone suffices as witness. Most report that the verse was revealed concerning Jews who denied knowing the Prophet, and Ibn Kathir also relates a narration in which Meccan leaders were involved. The overall meaning most commentators draw is a consolation for the Prophet and an affirmation of the truth of his mission.

This verse states that those who disbelieved in the Prophet ﷺ and his message, and turned others away from the path of God, have strayed very far from the truth. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Abu al-Su'ud, report that the verse primarily addresses the Jews, who concealed the description of the Prophet ﷺ found in their scriptures, told the polytheists they did not find it there, and claimed that prophethood could only come from the line of Aaron and David, or that Moses' law would never be abrogated. Al-Baydawi, al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that one who misleads others is more deeply lost than one who merely errs, since he combines his own error with leading others astray. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Sam'ani understand turning people away as concealing the Prophet's attributes. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress turning away from the truth and drawing others away from it too. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the 'far-off error' means it is hard to return from it. Ibn 'Ashur sees the phrase 'far' as a metaphor for extreme error, comparing it to distance. The commentators derive no legal rulings from this verse and mainly clarify its meaning and purpose.

This verse states that those who disbelieve and do wrong, persisting in disbelief, will not be forgiven while they remain in it, and God will not guide them to any path except the path of Hell, where they will remain forever, which is easy for God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya take disbelief and wrongdoing to go together, with wrongdoing understood as harming oneself through unbelief, concealing the Prophet's description, or turning people away from the truth. Al-Hasan and al-Baghawi suggest the address may include both Jews and Christians. Al-Zamakhshari restricts the wrongdoing to major sins, a view that Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi reject as departing from the plain context. Al-Wahidi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi apply the verse to those whom God knows will die in disbelief, while al-Razi makes it conditional on the absence of repentance. The commentators agree that the denied forgiveness excludes the guidance, and that the word path refers to religion or good deeds. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that this negative phrasing of refusal is stronger than a plain statement. Ibn 'Ashur reads the denial of guidance as a warning, with repentance still open, a position distinct from the literal reading of eternal punishment. Ibn 'Uthaymin explains that the guidance denied is the granting of success, and that the eternity is drawn from the word khulud.

The commentators explain that this verse refers to those who combined disbelief with wrongdoing. Most identify them as the Jews, while others understand them as idolaters or disbelievers in general. The meaning is that God will not forgive them or guide them to any path of salvation, the only path left to them being the path of Hell, where they will remain forever, and that this is easy for God, since nothing can thwart Him.

al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur largely agree that the denied forgiveness and guidance are tied to dying in disbelief without repentance, so the verse is a warning to those who persist in refusal. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di take the wrongdoing as an addition to disbelief, meaning obstinacy and hindering others from faith, whereas Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Shawkani mention other possible meanings, such as idolatry, concealing the Prophet's described qualities, or oppressing people by leading them astray.

al-Zamakhshari, followed by Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, read the verse as including grave sinners among the wrongdoers, who would then share the same eternal punishment. al-Alusi attributes this to the Mu'tazili position and rejects it on contextual grounds. al-Razi holds that the threat concerns those who die disbelieving, and that a condition of no repentance must be understood if the verse is taken in its full generality.

According to al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud, the "path" may mean any path leading to good, or only the path of truth, in which case the exception is disconnected. al-Jalalayn and al-Baydawi explain that "forever" excludes the sense of a long stay. Ibn 'Uthaymin, al-Jaza'iri and al-Qasimi emphasise that the verse states that obstinate disbelief closes the way to guidance, without denying that God may guide some of those people.

This verse addresses all of mankind, announcing that the Messenger Muhammad ﷺ has come to them with the truth from their Lord, so that believing in him is better for them. The commentators explain the truth variously as the Qur'an, as Islam, or as the testimony of monotheism. Al-Tabari adds that rejecting faith harms only the one who rejects it, since everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God. Most exegetes, including al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur, note that the address is general and that the message is meant for all people. On the grammar of the word 'better' (khayran), the scholars differ. Sibawayh and al-Khalil take it as the object of an omitted verb, meaning 'do what is better for you'. Al-Farra' takes it as a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, 'a faith that is better for you'. Al-Kisa'i and Abu Ubayda take it as the predicate of an omitted 'be', 'let faith be better for you'. Ibn Ashur finds the explanation by way of a circumstantial phrase more convincing, while Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi record the objections of the Basran grammarians to the omitted 'be'. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi stress that faith is good in this world and the next, and that disbelief harms only the disbeliever. These readings agree on the overall sense without settling the grammatical question.

God addresses the People of the Book, meaning mainly the Christians, forbidding them to go to excess in their religion, that is, to exceed the limit in exalting Jesus until they raised him above the rank of messenger, and forbidding them to say anything about God other than the truth, such as attributing to Him a son or a partner. He states that the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, is a messenger of God, His word which He cast to Mary, and a spirit from Him. The commentators differ on these terms. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the word as the command of creation, “Be”, and the spirit as a creature that God attributed to Himself out of honour. Al-Tabari also reports that the spirit is the breath Gabriel blew into Mary's garment, and that “from” marks origin rather than part, against the Christian claim. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that “from” indicates origin and that the spirit is so named for its purity, while others see mercy or revelation in it. God then orders them to believe in Him and His messengers, and forbids them to say “three”, since God is one God, exalted above having a son, for everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note that the Christian sects disagree on how the Trinity should be understood, and that the verse refutes all of these forms. The commentators agree that the verse forbids both excess and negligence, and that Jesus is God's servant and messenger, but they differ on the details of the meaning of the word and the spirit, and on whether the address concerns Christians alone or also Jews, as al-Hasan held.

This verse states that the Messiah does not disdain to be a servant of God, nor do the favoured angels, and that whoever turns away from worshipping God out of arrogance will be gathered to Him on the Day of Judgment. Most commentators distinguish istinkaf, a refusal mixed with haughty pride, from istikbar, a claim to greatness without that sense of disdain. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take the verse as a rebuttal of Christians who raised Jesus above the status of servant, and Ibn Kathir adds that the angels are mentioned because some took them as gods. Mu'tazilite scholars, al-Qadi Abu Bakr, al-Halimi and al-Zamakhshari used the verse to argue that angels are superior to prophets, while al-Razi, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Ashur replied that it does not necessarily prove this and that the question is open to reasoning. Al-Zamakhshari argued that the superiority meant is in strength and power rather than reward, a view developed further by al-Alusi and al-Qasimi, who also describe the debate on the sense of muqarrabun. Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud discuss the grammatical link of the coordinating particle with the Messiah. On the gathering, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi understand it as the resurrection, Ibn Kathir links it to God's just judgment, and Ibn Uthaymin notes that it includes all creatures. According to reports cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, the verse was revealed after a delegation from Najran objected that the Prophet was disparaging Jesus, and he answered that being a servant of God is no disgrace.

This verse sets out the fate of the two groups. As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, God will pay them their rewards in full and will add to them of His bounty, a bounty whose extent only God knows, which commentators illustrate with the saying that no eye has seen and no ear has heard. As for those who scorned to worship God and grew proud, He will punish them with a painful punishment, and they will find besides God neither a protector nor a helper. The commentators agree that the verse elaborates the recompense of the gathering mentioned just before, that istinkaf means refusing out of disdain and istikbar means arrogance, and that a good deed is multiplied at least tenfold, with some saying up to seven hundred times. Al-Tabari holds that the extra bounty has no fixed limit, while others restrict it to the multiplication already mentioned. Ibn Kathir quotes a report from Ibn Mas'ud about intercession for those who had done good to believers, but judges its chain weak while noting it is related from Ibn Mas'ud as a companion's statement. The verse is said to have been revealed concerning the delegation of Najran, who objected when the Prophet called Jesus a servant of God; the commentators explain that servanthood brings no shame. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya take the passage as evidence that angels are superior to prophets, whereas Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur deny that it proves this, and consider the matter a matter of scholarly judgment.

In this verse God addresses all people, telling them that a clear proof has come to them from their Lord and that He has sent down to them a manifest light. The commentators broadly agree on the meaning: "burhan" denotes a decisive and irrefutable proof, and the "manifest light" is the Quran, which reveals the truth just as light makes things visible.

Most exegetes identify the proof with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself, because of the miracles that attest to his truthfulness. This is the view of al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Najih, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, and al-Mawardi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi also report it. Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj take the burhan simply as argument or evidence without naming a person. Qatada and Ibn al-Jawzi, among others, identify it with the Quran, while al-Zamakhshari allows that it may mean the true religion or the Messenger.

Others understand it as Islam (Abu Hayyan), or as the whole body of signs of the mission, including rational proofs and transmitted testimony (al-Baydawi, Ibn Sa'di). Almost all commentators agree that the "light" refers to the Quran.

On the word "mubin", Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that it can mean both "clear in itself" and "making other things clear", and he holds that both meanings may be kept together since they do not conflict. Al-Sha'rawi stresses that the Quran's miracle is inseparable from its teaching, and that it addresses all humanity until the Hour.

This verse names the proof that has come from the Lord, which most commentators identify as the Prophet ﷺ, and the clear light He has sent down, which is the Quran. It then divides people into two groups. Those who believe in God and hold fast to Him will be admitted into His mercy and bounty, and He will guide them to a straight path. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, Ibn 'Ashur and others agree that the mercy and bounty refer to the Garden and its blessings, and that the straight path is Islam and obedience in this world, as well as the road to the Garden in the next. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi state that mercy is the Garden itself, while al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy take it more broadly as reward, elevation and spiritual joy.

The meaning of holding fast (i'tisam) is also debated. Ibn Jurayj understood it as holding to the Quran, as reported by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, whereas al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya explained it as seeking protection in God from Satan's deviation and human desires. As for the pronoun in 'to Him', Ibn 'Atiyya notes that it may refer to God or to the Quran, and Ibn Kathir and most commentators prefer God, though Ibn al-Jawzi reports that Muqatil also applied it to God.

Opinions differ on the nature of the guidance. Al-Hasan took it to mean provision in this world that leads to the bliss of the next, while others placed it in the hereafter, where believers are led to the road of the Garden. Ibn Kathir stresses that this path is clear and free of crookedness, and that believers walk it in both worlds. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur observe that the mention of grace shows that the reward is not a payment owed for deeds.

This verse answers the question put to the Prophet ﷺ about the kalala, the inheritance of a person who leaves neither descendants nor parents. God explains that if a man or a woman dies without children or parents and leaves a full or paternal sister, she receives half of the estate, and her brother inherits from her if she has no child. If there are two sisters, they receive two thirds, and when brothers and sisters are together, a male receives the share of two females. Al-Tabari reports that Abu Bakr defined the kalala as the one who leaves neither child nor parent, while in other reports Umar limited it to the absence of a father. Ibn Kathir notes that the majority view requires the absence of both descendants and ascendants. All agree that a sister does not inherit when a father is alive. However, Ibn Abbas and those who follow him, including Dawud al-Zahiri, hold that a sister does not inherit alongside a daughter, whereas the majority, including Ibn Mas'ud and Mu'adh, grant her half through agnatic inheritance. Al-Tabari also relates that Umar found this matter difficult and wished the Prophet had clarified it during his lifetime. On the closing phrase, the grammarians differ: the Basrans read it as 'out of fear that you go astray', while the Kufans understand an implied negation, which most commentators follow in meaning.
